Last Friday, after the spring science fair, I met Ms. Chen in the east hallway beside the equipment room to start the return before the building closed. The fair had used equipment from science classrooms, the art room, and the small greenhouse, and the boxes had been brought back in several trips because the cart could not fit through the greenhouse door. The main return was due Monday morning, but Ms. Chen wanted us to count everything on Friday so teachers could report anything still missing before the weekend. The return included materials that belonged to different departments, so we kept the labels visible and did not combine items just because they looked alike.

First, we cleared the long table by the sinks and put down a clean paper sheet for small pieces. The green crate held six hand lenses, three plastic trays, a roll of copper tape, and a sealed packet of bean seeds. The packet was still sealed, and Ms. Chen said it should go back to the greenhouse cabinet rather than to the science storeroom. The blue tub held two pairs of safety goggles. One had a loose strap, and the other had a scratched lens. The goggles with the scratched lens were usable for the demonstration but not for student use, so we put them in a separate bag with a note. The three thermometers were all there, and the red one still had its paper tag around the stem. We also found a glass jar with no lid and a lid with no matching jar, and kept them together in a box marked “Needs checking.”

1. Say the item, the location, and the person responsible for checking it. The small magnifiers came from Room 12, and Ms. Patel checked the count. The plastic trays came from the art room, and Mr. Lewis checked those. The seed packet and the watering gauge came from the greenhouse, and Ms. Chen checked them. The library aide will sign the return sheet because she is covering the front desk while the custodian checks the gym inventory. Ms. Chen will keep the duplicate copy until the aide has signed, and then the original goes into the office envelope. We wrote the corrected responsibility in the margin before making the final copy.

We counted eight extension leads, but only seven were in the coil bag. One was on the display table beside the model volcano, and Mr. Lewis brought it over before we finished the count. The orange lead had a small split near the plug, and we did not test it. We marked it “Do not use” and left it on the table for the science department chair to inspect. The power strip had six outlets, and its switch worked when we checked it. There was also a cardboard sign that said, “Please do not move the model until the glue is dry.” The volcano was dry by Friday, but the sign had a handwritten note on the back about returning the black gravel to Room 12, so we kept the note with the model instead of throwing it away.

Ms. Chen read the label on the storage cabinet aloud: “Return the lenses in their cloth sleeves and leave the calibration card in the top drawer.” The sleeves were in a small envelope in the cabinet, and there were five of them although we had counted six hand lenses, so we checked the science prep room and found the last sleeve in a drying rack. We did not find the calibration card in the top drawer at first. It was inside the blue folder on the shelf above the cabinet. Ms. Chen moved it back into the drawer after checking the number printed on it. The drawer also held two old batteries that were not part of the fair equipment, and we left them there rather than adding them to the return list.

For the art room return, Mr. Lewis counted twelve brushes and nine mixing palettes. The brushes were dry, but two palettes still had a thin layer of blue paint, so he put those beside the sink with a note for the art teacher. The paper lantern frames were stacked flat with tissue between them, and one frame had a bent corner. Mr. Lewis said he would show it to the art teacher before deciding whether it could be stored with the others. The greenhouse watering gauge was clean and its scale was readable, but the plastic clip was cracked. Ms. Chen said if the greenhouse teacher wants to reuse the gauge, the teacher should replace the clip first; otherwise, it should stay in the small repair box until the next equipment review. We attached a note stating that condition to the gauge.

Before we closed the equipment room, we checked the return sheet against the labels one more time. The entries for the Room 12 materials were on the first page, and the art and greenhouse entries were on the second page. The blue tub and the bag with the damaged goggles had separate lines so no one would mistake them for ordinary usable supplies. We put the sealed seed packet in a dry envelope and placed it on the greenhouse shelf. The jar and loose lid remained in the “Needs checking” box because we could not tell whether they belonged together. The orange extension lead stayed out of the coil bag, and the note about the volcano gravel stayed with the model.

I carried the office envelope to the front desk but did not leave it there because the library aide was helping a parent and had not signed yet. Ms. Chen kept the duplicate copy, and I took the original back to the equipment room for the night. The aide can sign it Monday morning before the returned supplies are distributed, and the custodian can check the gym inventory separately. If the office is still locked when we arrive, the original should remain with Ms. Chen until the desk opens. We left the table clear except for the bagged goggles, the orange lead, the repair box, and the model with its handwritten gravel note, and Ms. Chen locked the equipment room after we checked that the greenhouse shelf was dry.

at the top, customers should choose pickup or delivery, then give their name, phone number, and email address. the phone number is the best way to contact them if a detail is missing, but we still need the email for the written confirmation. the delivery option is available only within the bakery's local delivery area, which is printed on a separate map linked beside the choice. if a customer selects delivery and enters an address outside that area, the form should not accept the delivery selection; it should ask the customer to choose pickup instead. don't hide the pickup choice in that situation. a delivery address field should appear only after delivery is chosen, while pickup customers should not have to fill in an address.

we need the requested date and a time window on every order. for pickup, the choices are 9:00–11:00 a.m., 11:00 a.m.–1:00 p.m., and 1:00–3:00 p.m. for delivery, the choices are 10:00 a.m.–noon and noon–2:00 p.m. the time choices should change with the service choice so someone does not see a pickup window on a delivery order. if a customer selects pickup and submits the form by 3 p.m. at least two business days before the requested date, staff should hold the selected pickup window. if either the 3 p.m. cutoff or the two-business-day lead time is missed, staff should not promise that window and should offer the next available pickup window instead. the same cutoff rule is not a promise that an order is accepted; the bakery still has to check the items and confirm the order.

for delivery, the form should show a note that deliveries are scheduled in the two listed windows, not at an exact minute. a customer can enter a preferred delivery window, but that preference is subject to route capacity. if the preferred window is full, staff should offer the other listed window before they confirm. if neither window can be used on that date, staff should contact the customer to ask whether another date works; do not move the date without asking. delivery charges are calculated from the address and appear in the order total before payment. pickup has no delivery charge. customers can pay by card online or select pay at pickup for pickup orders; pay at pickup should not appear for delivery orders.

next, the form needs an item section that lets a customer add several lines to one order. for each line, ask for the product name, quantity, and any size or serving choice that applies. cake sizes are 6-inch, 8-inch, and 10-inch; the serving estimates beside them are 8, 12, and 20 portions. pastry boxes come in 6-piece and 12-piece sizes, while bread is ordered by loaf. these choices should only be displayed for the relevant product, rather than shown together as if a loaf had a cake size. catered trays are listed in small and large sizes, and staff will confirm the serving estimate for those after they review the order.

cake customers should have a separate space for flavor, filling, and decoration notes. the standard cake flavors are vanilla, chocolate, and lemon, and the fillings are raspberry, chocolate ganache, and vanilla cream. decoration notes are requests, not a guarantee that every design can be made. the form should say, “Please describe the colors or theme you have in mind; we will confirm what we can provide.” if a customer asks for writing on a cake, include a text field with a 30-character limit. the limit applies to the writing only, not to the decoration notes. pastry box customers can list up to three pastry types in the notes field, but the form should not imply that every type is available every day.

we also need a clearly worded allergy field. customers can identify an allergy or enter “none,” and the form must not treat a blank allergy field as the same as “none.” a note beside it should say that the bakery handles wheat, eggs, milk, peanuts, and tree nuts in the same kitchen. if a customer reports an allergy, the form should flag the order for staff review before confirmation. that flag does not itself mean the bakery can safely prepare the order, and the confirmation message should not promise an allergy-free product. customers should be able to add other dietary notes, but those notes should stay separate from the allergy response.

1. order review and confirmation
before payment, show the customer a review with service type, date, window, address when applicable, each item and quantity, notes, charges, and total. if a customer uses pay at pickup, show the amount due without asking for card details. the submit button should say “Send order request,” since sending the form does not mean the bakery has accepted the order. after submission, show, “Your request has been received. We will contact you after reviewing availability and details.” the emailed copy should include the requested date and all entered notes, so the customer and staff can check the same information.

staff need the submitted order to show when it arrived, whether the customer chose pickup or delivery, and whether an allergy response was entered. orders arriving by counter entry should retain the time staff entered them, not the time the customer first came into the shop. this matters for the two-business-day pickup check: staff use the system entry time to decide whether the cutoff has been met. the form should not automatically label an order late or reject it based only on the requested date, because staff may need to discuss a different date or window with the customer. keep the originally requested date visible even if the customer later agrees to a change.

customers sometimes need to correct an order after sending it. the confirmation email should tell them to call the bakery rather than submit a second form, and the staff record should keep the initial request visible alongside any change agreed to by phone. if an order has not yet been confirmed, staff can update its details after speaking with the customer; if it has been confirmed, staff should first check whether the requested change is still possible. the form itself should not claim that an edit has been made just because someone called. this distinction is important when an item, delivery address, or requested window changes, since the kitchen and delivery list use the confirmed details.

please keep the page readable on a phone, with short labels and the explanation placed beside the relevant field. the separate delivery-area map should remain linked near the service choice, and the allergy note should be visible before a customer submits. we do not need a promotional message or a long description of the bakery on this form. the goal is for customers to enter a complete request, understand what is only a preference, and know that staff will review the order before it is confirmed. the final wording should work for online customers and for staff entering a counter order, including when the customer needs to be contacted about a date, window, or allergy response.

hey folks, can someone do the ventilation check in the woodshop before the afternoon class on thursday? the facilities sheet says the extraction fans were serviced monday, but we still need to check them at the bench and spray booth, not just tick the sheet. please note the airflow reading at both points and whether the paper strip pulls steadily toward each grille. if both readings are at least 8 air changes per hour and there's no visible dust hanging around either area, leave both areas open for class and add the numbers to the log. otherwise, if either reading is under 8 or dust is still hanging around that point, close only the affected area and put a note on the door. don't run the spray booth if its own check doesn't pass; the bench can still be used if its reading meets the limit and there's no dust there. if the booth passes but the bench doesn't, keep the bench closed and use the booth only if there's no dust there either. could you post the readings here too? thanks!
payload.response: Hey folks, can someone do the ventilation check in the woodshop before the afternoon class on Thursday? The facilities sheet says the extraction fans were serviced Monday, but we still need to check them at the bench and spray booth, not just tick the sheet. Please note the airflow reading at both points and whether the paper strip pulls steadily toward each grille. If both readings are at least 8 air changes per hour and there's no visible dust hanging around either area, leave both areas open for class and add the numbers to the log. Otherwise, if either reading is under 8 or dust is still hanging around that point, close only the affected area and put a note on the door. Don't run the spray booth if its own check doesn't pass; the bench can still be used if its reading meets the limit and there's no dust there. If the booth passes but the bench doesn't, keep the bench closed and use the booth only if there's no dust there either. Could you post the readings here too? Thanks!

We are putting together the Cedar Lane Seed Exchange for Saturday, May 18, at the old Grange Hall on Mill Road, and this is the planning talk from Tuesday evening, not a public announcement yet. The doors are supposed to open at nine, and the tables will be ready by 8:15. The hall manager said the side entrance can be unlocked at eight if someone from our group is there to meet him; otherwise, everybody has to use the front steps. The ramp is on the north side, and we should leave that route clear because two regular visitors use walkers. The exchange is free, and people can bring saved seeds or take packets without bringing anything. The idea is to make it friendly for first-time gardeners as well as people who have been growing here for years.

The room has twelve folding tables, and we have permission to use ten of them. The other two need to stay against the west wall for the quilting group that meets in the afternoon. Please put the vegetable packets near the windows because the light is good there, but keep them out of direct sun if the curtains are open. The herb table will be beside the water fountain, and flowers will go across from the entrance. We need a clear aisle from the door to the back of the room and a smaller gap between each table so people can move without brushing the displays. The hall has three extension cords, but we should only use one for the label printer and tape it along the wall, not across a walking route.

The exchange team has four main jobs, and I want to say them slowly: first, receiving and checking packets; second, setting up the tables; third, greeting people and keeping track of shared supplies; and fourth, closing the room and returning the key. Priya is the packet lead, and Noah is checking the sign-in sheets. Priya will bring the blank labels and the small scale, and she will sort anything with no crop name into a question box rather than guessing what it is. Sam is handling the table plan and has a printed map in the green folder. Jo is greeting people at the front table, and I will keep the supply list and be available if a volunteer needs a break.

For receiving packets, we want the plant name, the variety if known, the year collected, and the name of the person who saved them. Packets should be dry and sealed and should have enough seeds for at least five small gardens. If someone brings a large envelope, Priya can divide it after asking them first. We are not refusing packets just because the handwriting is hard to read. She can ask the donor or write a question mark on the label if nobody knows the variety. Please do not describe a seed as organic unless the person who saved it says that is accurate, and do not promise that a packet will grow in every yard. We can offer general information, but the weather and soil make a difference.

The three supplies we still need to borrow are a folding hand truck, two extra marker pens, and a small tablecloth for the welcome desk. We have enough paper bags but only about forty blank labels, so Priya will print another sheet on Thursday evening. Sam has offered to bring masking tape and scissors, and the library is lending us two clipboards. The packet count from the storage cabinet is 1,138, but some of those packets are herbs that need a closer check. The printed inventory says 963 vegetable packets, and the handwritten notebook lists 175 flowers and herbs. Those totals match for now, but we should count the question box separately and not include it in the public totals.

When people arrive, Jo can say, “Take what you will use and leave some for the next person.” We are not asking visitors to fill out a form, and there is no limit per person at the moment. If the room gets crowded, she can ask people to step aside while another visitor reaches the table, but we should not start enforcing a packet limit unless the organizers talk it through together. The neighborhood garden club may bring six children around 10:30, and their teacher has asked whether they can sit at one end of the flower table while they sort their packets. We can make room for them if the aisle stays open and an adult remains with the group.

First, for the morning setup, lay down the table map and check the aisle. Second, put the signs on the right tables and place the question box beside Priya. Third, set out packets with the labels facing up and leave the handwritten inventory in the green folder. Fourth, keep the welcome desk clear except for the clipboards and a cup for spare pencils. At 11:30, someone should check whether the water jug needs filling, and after lunch we should gather loose labels and return markers to the supply box. Those are reminders rather than extra jobs, and nobody needs to leave their station unattended to do them.

One condition that matters is the forecast. If there is heavy rain before 8:30, we will not put the two outdoor display boards on the pavement, even if the sky clears later, because the boards can become slippery and the hall manager asked us to protect the floor. In that case, we can put the garden club poster inside by the noticeboard. If there is only light rain, the boards may go under the covered porch as long as the front entrance remains unobstructed. Sam is checking the forecast Friday evening and will text the team, but that message is only about the boards, not a change to the opening time.

At closing, we need to leave the ten tables folded only after the packets and supplies are collected, and the west wall must remain clear for the quilting group. We should return the key to the lockbox by 4:15 and send the manager a message once the door is locked. Any seeds that remain can go back into the labeled storage tubs on the top shelf, except the question box, which stays separate until Priya has checked with the donors. If someone leaves a phone number with a packet question, Jo can put that note in the green folder, and we can follow up after the exchange. The final count and a note about any missing supplies belong in the notebook before we leave.

i need a small command-line utility for cleaning up old log files in one folder. It should take the folder path and a number of days as inputs, and look only at regular files directly in that folder whose names end in .log, not walk into subfolders. Compare each file's last-modified time with the cutoff based on the supplied day count. If a .log file is older than the cutoff and there is a sibling file with the same base name ending in .log.gz, delete the .log file; if either part of that condition isn't true, leave that .log file alone. It should leave the .log.gz files alone and not rename or rewrite file contents. Please print a short report at the end with deleted filenames and filenames of .log files left alone, and say how many are in each group. If the path doesn't exist or the day count isn't a positive whole number, print a useful error and stop before changing anything. Keep the implementation simple, show the complete code and a brief run example. don't add a scheduler or make it run automatically.
payload.response:
Create a small command-line utility to clean up old log files in a single folder.

- Accept a folder path and a number of days as inputs. Look only at regular files directly in that folder whose names end in `.log`; do not search subfolders.
- Compare each `.log` file’s last-modified time with the cutoff calculated from the supplied day count. Delete a file only if it is older than the cutoff **and** a sibling file with the same base name ending in `.log.gz` exists. Otherwise, leave the `.log` file alone. In particular, keep newer files and files without a matching compressed sibling.
- Leave `.log.gz` files alone, and do not rename files or rewrite their contents.
- At the end, print a short report listing the deleted filenames and the filenames of `.log` files left alone, with a count for each group.
- If the folder path does not exist or the day count is not a positive whole number, print a useful error and stop before changing anything.

Keep the implementation simple. Provide the complete code and a brief example of how to run it. Do not add a scheduler or make the utility run automatically.

LANGUAGE: en

INPUT:
i’m writing this field notebook entry for the west bench traverse on 18 june, above alder creek in the north fork range. i was the person taking the notes and making the measurements; Elias Ward came with me to carry the sample bags and mark the stops on the route map. We started at 7:40 a.m. from the old forestry gate, at an elevation of about 1,460 metres, with low cloud over the ridge but no rain. The purpose was to check the sandstone contact mapped last autumn and see whether the narrow band could be followed toward the creek. The notebook is mine, although Elias wrote the labels on the sample bags while I called out the station numbers.

The first exposure was a road cut roughly 300 metres east of the gate. I described the sandstone as fine-grained, grey-brown, and mostly in thin beds, with a few rusty streaks along the joints. The bedding dipped 28 degrees toward the southeast, measured with my compass clinometer, and the cut was about six metres high at its tallest point. There were loose blocks at the base, so we stayed on the road shoulder rather than climbing onto the face. Elias held the ranging pole at the lower contact while I checked the angle, then he put a small flag beside the point we used. The flag was orange, not the pink one shown in my older map notes.

At station WB-02, the sandstone gave way to a darker, finer layer that I first called siltstone in my notes. On closer inspection it had a slight sheen and split along very flat surfaces, so I changed the description to shale, not siltstone. I crossed out the first word once and left it readable underneath because I want the correction to show what I thought in the field. The shale layer was about 40 centimetres thick where it was exposed, but the lower edge disappeared beneath moss and gravel. I could not see whether it continued as a single bed around the bend, and I did not measure a contact that was hidden.

Elias collected two pieces from loose material below the cut, and I watched him put them in separate bags rather than combining them. He marked one WB-02A and the other WB-02B, then wrote the date and his initials on both labels. The first piece was a fresh grey chip with a small white vein; the second was weathered brown on one side and had no visible vein. I asked Elias whether either chip had come directly from the bed, and he said, “No, both were already down at the base.” That means the bags are useful examples from the exposure, but they are not samples taken in place.

We followed the contact east for another 180 metres, where alder roots and a shallow ditch interrupted the view. At WB-03 I noted a patch of pale green mineral stain on a joint surface, about the size of my hand. I did not identify the mineral, since the color alone was not enough and I had no hand lens with me that morning. A short distance farther on, the sandstone beds appeared thicker, around 10 to 15 centimetres, though the outcrop was broken and partly covered. Elias measured the distance between the two flagged stops on the map, while I checked the route against the contour lines; our estimate was 180 metres, not a pace count.

The creek crossing was low enough to step over at the marked boulder, but the stones on the north bank were slick. We crossed one at a time, with Elias going first and holding the pack strap while I stepped across. The water was clear and roughly ankle deep at the crossing; I did not take a temperature reading because the thermometer had been left in the vehicle. On the far side, the contact seemed to turn north, but the next 25 metres were hidden by brush. I wrote “possible north turn” in the margin rather than drawing a continuous line. If we return after the brush is cut back, we should check whether the band actually bends north or simply disappears beneath the slope debris.

I also noted the weather because it affects the paper and the exposed surfaces. The cloud lifted around 10:15, and a brief gust dried the wet corners of the map, but the notebook pages stayed dry. The west-facing rock was still damp in the shade, so its darker color may not match the drier face near the road cut. At 11:05, I compared the compass bearing on my field sketch with the route map and found a difference of about five degrees. I have not changed the sketch bearing yet; the compass may have shifted when I set the map beside the metal buckle on my pack. I want to check it away from the pack before treating either bearing as final.

1. WB-01 is the road-cut exposure east of the forestry gate; orange flag placed by Elias at the lower contact.
2. WB-02 is the shale layer in the cut; thickness approximately 40 centimetres where visible, with its lower edge covered.
3. WB-02A and WB-02B are loose pieces collected by Elias below the cut, not in-place samples.
4. WB-03 is the green-stained joint surface farther east; mineral identification remains open.
5. The apparent north turn near the creek is uncertain because brush and slope debris block the view.

I asked Nia Bell, the project archivist, to scan these pages and attach the route map to the same record, rather than filing the map separately. If the notebook paper is still damp when she receives it, I asked her to wait until it is dry before scanning, since the corners curl and the pencil notes are harder to read when they are wet. I have not asked her to interpret the green stain or revise the map. The field sketch includes the three station labels, the orange flag, and the creek crossing, but it does not show the exact position of the two loose sample pieces. Elias’s bag labels and the map should stay with the entry so the sample locations are not mistaken for bedrock collection points.

Before leaving the west bench, we checked the gate-side route once more and found no additional exposure between WB-01 and the gravel pullout. The notebook records the time as 11:40 a.m. when we reached the vehicle, and the sample bags were still separate and dry. I packed the compass in the outer pocket, away from the metal buckle, for the check at the next stop. The final page has a small blank area below the station list for any bearing correction after that check; I have left it blank for now. The creek-side contact remains a field observation to revisit, and the sketch should not be read as proof that the band continues around the bend.

There were loose blocks at the base, so we stayed on the road shoulder rather than climbing onto the face. Elias held the ranging pole at the lower contact while I checked the angle, then put a small flag beside the point we used. The flag was orange, not the pink one shown in my older map notes.

At station WB-02, the sandstone gave way to a darker, finer layer that I first called siltstone in my notes. On closer inspection, it had a slight sheen and split along very flat surfaces, so I changed the description to shale, not siltstone. I crossed out the first word once and left it readable underneath because I want the correction to show what I thought in the field. The shale layer was about 40 centimetres thick where exposed, but the lower edge disappeared beneath moss and gravel. I couldn’t see whether it continued as a single bed around the bend, and I did not measure a contact that was hidden.

Elias collected two pieces from loose material below the cut, and I watched him put them in separate bags rather than combining them. He marked one WB-02A and the other WB-02B, then wrote the date and his initials on both labels. The first piece was a fresh grey chip with a small white vein; the second was weathered brown on one side and had no visible vein. I asked Elias whether either chip had come directly from the bed, and he said, “No, both were already down at the base.” That means the bags are useful examples from the exposure, but they are not samples taken in place.

We followed the contact east for another 180 metres, where alder roots and a shallow ditch interrupted the view. At WB-03, I noted a patch of pale green mineral stain on a joint surface, about the size of my hand. I did not identify the mineral, since color alone wasn’t enough and I had no hand lens with me that morning. A short distance farther on, the sandstone beds appeared thicker, around 10 to 15 centimetres, though the outcrop was broken and partly covered. Elias measured the distance between the two flagged stops on the map while I checked the route against the contour lines. Our estimate was 180 metres, not a pace count.

The creek crossing was low enough to step over at the marked boulder, but the stones on the north bank were slick. We crossed one at a time, with Elias going first and holding the pack strap while I stepped across. The water was clear and roughly ankle-deep at the crossing. I did not take a temperature reading because the thermometer had been left in the vehicle. On the far side, the contact seemed to turn north, but the next 25 metres were hidden by brush. I wrote “possible north turn” in the margin rather than drawing a continuous line. If we return after the brush is cut back, we should check whether the band actually bends north or simply disappears beneath the slope debris.

I also noted the weather because it affects the paper and the exposed surfaces. The cloud lifted around 10:15, and a brief gust dried the wet corners of the map, but the notebook pages stayed dry. The west-facing rock was still damp in the shade, so its darker color may not match the drier face near the road cut. At 11:05, I compared the compass bearing on my field sketch with the route map and found a difference of about five degrees. I haven’t changed the sketch bearing yet; the compass may have shifted when I set the map beside the metal buckle on my pack. I want to check it away from the pack before treating either bearing as final.

1. WB-01 is the road-cut exposure east of the forestry gate; Elias placed the orange flag at the lower contact.
2. WB-02 is the shale layer in the cut; it is approximately 40 centimetres thick where visible, with its lower edge covered.
3. WB-02A and WB-02B are loose pieces Elias collected below the cut, not in-place samples.
4. WB-03 is the green-stained joint surface farther east; mineral identification remains open.
5. The apparent north turn near the creek is uncertain because brush and slope debris block the view.

I asked Nia Bell, the project archivist, to scan these pages and attach the route map to the same record rather than filing the map separately. If the notebook paper is still damp when she receives it, I asked her to wait until it is dry before scanning, since the corners curl and the pencil notes are harder to read when wet. I haven’t asked her to interpret the green stain or revise the map. The field sketch includes the three station labels, the orange flag, and the creek crossing, but it does not show the exact position of the two loose sample pieces. Elias’s bag labels and the map should stay with the entry so the sample locations are not mistaken for bedrock collection points.

Before leaving the west bench, we checked the gate-side route once more and found no additional exposure between WB-01 and the gravel pullout. The notebook records the time as 11:40 a.m. when we reached the vehicle, and the sample bags were still separate and dry. I packed the compass in the outer pocket, away from the metal buckle, for the check at the next stop. The final page has a small blank area below the station list for any bearing correction after that check; I’ve left it blank for now. The creek-side contact remains a field observation to revisit, and the sketch should not be read as proof that the band continues around the bend.

We don’t want it silently opening last week’s download, even if that file happens to have the same name.

LANGUAGE: en

INPUT:
i’m writing about the estimate for my Aster M4 camera, serial AM4-78126, which I left with North Quay Camera Service on 26 May. I need a clear itemized estimate before deciding what to do. The camera was purchased in 2021, and the shutter count shown on its menu is 18,640. Please keep the estimate tied to this camera and distinguish the inspection findings from possible repairs. I’m not authorizing any work by asking for the estimate.

The main problem is that the camera sometimes fails to power on after it has been in my bag for several hours. When it does turn on, the top display comes on, but the rear screen can stay black. The problem is intermittent rather than constant. I tested it at home with each of my 2 batteries, and it happened with both, although not every time. One battery is the original Aster battery and the other is a replacement from the same maker. I have not tested the camera with another charger, so I don’t know whether charging is part of the problem.

There is also a separate issue with the control dial on the back. It turns, but some changes to the menu selection do not register unless I turn it slowly and try again. The shutter button still takes a picture when the camera is on. I have not noticed a crack in the body or damage to the lens mount. I told the intake person that I did not want those details treated as proof of a particular fault; they are just what I have observed. The technician said, “We’ll check the power issue and the dial before we put a repair amount on paper.” Please include the technician’s inspection results in the estimate, even if the results are inconclusive.

For context, the camera was in my carry-on during a rainy weekend in March, but it stayed inside a closed bag and I did not see water on it. I’m mentioning that because the intake form asks about moisture, not because I know that moisture caused anything. The camera has not been dropped, to my knowledge. The last time I cleaned it was in April, using a dry cloth on the outside only. I have not opened the body or tried to repair it myself. Please avoid stating that there is water damage or impact damage unless the inspection actually supports that finding.

I also want the estimate to make it clear which charges are for work already performed and which are only possible future charges. I understand that the shop may need to inspect the camera to identify the fault, but I do not know whether the initial inspection fee is already included in the estimate I received at intake. Please list that fee separately and say whether it is charged even if I decline a repair. The intake person gave me a printed receipt but did not give me a repair price or a completion date, so I am not asking you to confirm either one from that conversation.

Please organize the estimate around these items, with the description and amount for each one where it can be determined:
1. The inspection and diagnosis of the intermittent power problem, including whether the camera behaves differently with either battery.
2. The inspection of the rear control dial and any cleaning or adjustment that may be proposed for it.
3. Any parts that might be needed, listed separately from labor, with the part name and whether it is new or refurbished if that information is available.
4. Labor for each proposed repair, rather than one unexplained combined amount.
5. Any additional fee, including the initial inspection fee, and whether it applies if I decide not to proceed.

The main studio is in the North Quay building, and the small production room is available when no recording is booked there.

The weekday morning schedule starts with the local bulletin at 6:30, followed by First Light with Inez Park from 7:00 to 9:00. Inez has confirmed the time, and she will take the news handover from the bulletin reader at seven. The 9:00 slot is Open Table, a call-in program hosted by Lewis Grant, and the current plan is for Lewis to use the production room for the first half hour while the main studio is reset. At 10:00, the music desk takes over with a recorded set prepared by volunteers. The noon bulletin stays at noon; it is not being moved to make room for a longer interview. On Tuesday, the local council segment is scheduled inside Open Table, from 9:20 to 9:35, and Lewis has agreed to take the questions in that segment.

The afternoon pattern is the same on all five weekdays unless a program is listed separately. At 1:00, Field Notes is hosted by Aria Bell, who records short reports about gardens, waterways, and public transport. Her Friday edition will be live, since she has booked the main studio for that hour. The regular 2:00 music program, Small Frequencies, is presented by Niko James and uses the station’s locally made music library. Niko has asked Mara to keep the last ten minutes open on Wednesday for a short conversation with a visiting record-shop owner; Mara has placed a hold there, but the guest has not confirmed. At 3:00, the schedule returns to the volunteer music desk. The 4:30 bulletin is read by whoever is listed on the daily staffing sheet, rather than by a single regular presenter.

After the evening bulletin, the schedule includes a mix of live and recorded programs. On Monday, Sound Map runs from 6:00 to 7:00, with recordings supplied by the station’s neighborhood contributors. The Tuesday 6:00 slot is still marked for a repeat of the Saturday arts interview, because the original file is already cleared for another broadcast. On Wednesday, the youth program Back Steps is live from 6:00 to 6:45, and host Samira Cole has asked to keep the phone line open for listener questions. I have left the next fifteen minutes unassigned rather than extending the show without her agreement. Thursday’s 6:00 program is a recorded conversation about the history of the ferry terminal. On Friday, the 7:00 slot is reserved for the monthly volunteer meeting broadcast, with the meeting expected to finish by 8:00; the overnight music sequence begins at 8:00 as usual.

He also told me, “The cooling fan is louder than last month, but the readings stayed within the usual range.” Tom has not asked for a schedule change, and his note does not say that the fan has failed. He proposed a maintenance visit for Thursday, June 5, between 5:30 and 6:30 p.m., when the building is usually quiet. The visit is not yet in the engineering diary because the building caretaker has not confirmed access. I have kept the Thursday ferry-terminal program in its normal 6:00 slot for now. If the visit runs past 6:30, Tom says the station should use the backup studio for the bulletin and delay the recorded program until 6:45; if it finishes on time, the listed schedule stays in place. Please do not enter either change unless the visit is confirmed and the timing condition applies.

1. On Wednesday, Niko’s requested conversation is only a hold, not a confirmed guest booking. Should I leave the final ten minutes of Small Frequencies open, or restore the regular music selection if the guest has not confirmed by Tuesday at noon? Niko asked Mara for the hold, and Mara is asking Priya which schedule treatment to use. I have not told Niko that either option has been approved.
2. For Saturday, Daniel Cho has proposed a one-hour archive feature at 10:00 a.m. in place of the usual volunteer music desk. Daniel has a set of recordings from the station’s first year, but he has not delivered the edited program. Should I reserve the slot provisionally until Friday, or keep the regular desk in the grid? Daniel proposed the feature to Mara; this is not yet a request from the volunteer desk to give up its slot.
3. The Sunday 4:00 community noticeboard currently has two possible readers, Jo Price and Malik Ford. Jo told me she can read it if she is back from the market by 3:30, while Malik has said he is available for the whole afternoon. Please tell me whether to list Malik as the confirmed reader and Jo as the alternate, or to leave both names pending until Sunday morning. I have not asked either person to swap with the other.

The Saturday schedule otherwise starts with the 8:00 local bulletin, followed by the volunteer music desk from 8:30 to 10:00. At 11:00, the monthly repair clinic has a recorded slot, and its organizer has sent the running order but has not asked for a live phone-in. The afternoon includes a two-hour program of listener-selected records, with requests collected by email through Friday. Sunday has the neighborhood calendar at 9:00, a recorded nature program at 11:00, and the community noticeboard at 4:00. The noticeboard is limited to local events that organizers have submitted by Saturday evening; it is not a general call for announcements. Both weekend overnight sequences use the same cleared library as the weekday sequence, and the station’s final bulletin of the week is Sunday at 6:00 p.m. The production room booking board shows a children’s choir recording on Saturday from 1:00 to 2:00, so that room should not be listed as available during that hour.

delivery-summary.tsv

Dev: I’ve added that file name to the handover notes so everyone can find the delivery record from the shared drive. If a delivery is missing from the list, we should check with the office before assuming it was left at the gate.

Maya: The noticeboard is getting crowded, so I moved the lost-property note below the opening hours. There are two gloves in the clear tray, one silver bottle, and a small front light with a cracked clip. None has a name on it. I’ll keep them there through the end of the month, then take the unclaimed items to the office cupboard for the usual collection.

Jon: I also labeled the wall hooks by size: helmets on the top row, locks in the middle, and reusable shopping bags on the bottom. Those hooks are for temporary items, not long-term storage, so please clear anything that’s still there at the end of each week. The grey helmet belongs to the maintenance team and stays on the top hook; it has a white sticker inside the rim.

Rina: Saturday’s forecast looks dry until mid-afternoon, so I’ve penciled in 10:30 for the gate-stop check. i’m Lena Ortiz, and i coordinate the weekly schedule at Harbor Signal, an independent radio station in Bellwether. I’m preparing next week’s grid, which covers Monday, June 9, through Sunday, June 15. The station broadcasts from a small studio above the Bellwether Public Market, and our schedule is posted on the station website and on a noticeboard at the library. I have placed the local news bulletin at 6:30 each evening because the host is available then, and the slot is already confirmed.

For the Wednesday program, I proposed moving the community interview from 7:00 to 7:30 p.m. so the youth music hour can use the studio before it. That change is still a proposal, not a confirmed schedule item. Dev Shah, our sound engineer, checked the studio booking and found that it is free at 7:30 on Wednesday. I asked Nina Park, the volunteer producer for the community interview, to tell me whether the guest can arrive at the later time. Nina has not replied yet. If the guest cannot make 7:30, I will leave the interview in its current slot. I also asked Nina to send the updated program description to Jo Bell at the library, who maintains the noticeboard, but I have not asked Jo to change the schedule before the time is settled.

payload.instruction:
MODE: /prompt
LANGUAGE: en
INPUT:
make me a clear prompt for a writing task about the north stair rehearsal archive. it's a fictional community orchestra archive and the task is to ask for an internal cataloging and access plan, not a history or a public announcement. the archive is based in a former school music room in a port neighborhood. it has rehearsal recordings from 2008 through 2022, mostly amateur digital files, a smaller group of minidiscs, and twelve cassette tapes that have not been digitized. the orchestra rehearsed weekly during the season, but some years have gaps because the room was closed for repairs. don't make the archive sound bigger or more complete than it is.

the plan should help two volunteer archivists keep files findable and decide what can be shared. they have about four hours a week between them, one shared laptop, and no dedicated server. the current folder structure was made by different people over time, so dates and ensemble names aren't consistent. there are 186 digital audio files in the main folder, including duplicates and a few exports with no original file alongside them. another 41 files are on two old external drives; their contents have not been checked against the main folder. the twelve cassettes are in paper sleeves, with handwritten dates on only seven. don't imply anyone has listened to or inventoried the material already if that isn't stated.

use the following facts as the basis for practical recommendations. the orchestra usually had 18 to 26 players, and the same rehearsal might include a full ensemble, a woodwind group, or a smaller string section. there are no reliable attendance sheets. some filenames use the date first, some use a piece title, and some say things like “final take” without saying what was recorded. the conductor's name is printed on programs, but programs survive for only about half the years. there are 9 programs in a folder marked “old concert things,” and nobody knows whether it is complete. avoid treating those programs as proof of who attended a particular rehearsal.

i need a usable internal plan, not a software shopping list or a promise to process everything. mention a simple naming approach, a small set of metadata fields, a way to identify likely duplicates, and a sequence the volunteers could follow without making a huge project. fit the recommendations to their limited time and equipment. don't claim that file checksums, transcription, or audio cleanup are already happening. the plan should separate what they can do now from what would need more time or expertise. don't decide which old recordings are musically important, and don't rank the performances.

include the following exact remarks as examples of descriptions that should remain attributed to their sources, rather than being converted into verified catalog facts. the handwritten note on one minidisc says, “Nov 2014? winds, second half maybe.” a paper sleeve on cassette 3 says, “Mira says this is the winter concert run-through, not sure which year.” an email from a former player, received with the drive, says, “I think the room microphones were moved after the boiler work, but I can’t remember when.” keep the wording and uncertainty in each remark exactly as written. the plan should explain how such notes can be recorded as source notes, with their source identified, without silently resolving uncertain dates, group types, or equipment history.

there is also an access issue that must be handled carefully. for recordings made after 2018, a consent form exists for some sessions but the archive has not matched every form to a recording. one former player has asked that their voice not be placed online, but the archivists do not yet know which files include that player. if a session's consent form cannot be matched, the plan should say to hold that session back from online sharing while allowing internal preservation work to continue. if the player can be identified in a recording, don't propose publishing that file until the request is reviewed with them. for older recordings, there is no uniform release paperwork; the plan should describe that uncertainty, not assume blanket permission or blanket refusal. keep public sharing decisions distinct from internal cataloging.

please organize the requested prompt so it asks for an internal plan with a short purpose statement, practical workflow, and clear cautions. it should ask for a suggested filename pattern and a compact metadata list, but not prescribe a specific database or platform. ask the writer to use only the facts given here and label proposed steps as recommendations rather than completed work. keep the advice realistic for two volunteers and avoid legal conclusions. the final plan should be useful even though the archive is incomplete and unevenly documented.

1) make sure the prompt asks the writer to cover these in a numbered section: first, an initial inventory of the main folder, external drives, minidiscs and cassettes; second, a cautious method for comparing duplicates without deleting anything; third, a small metadata record that can distinguish a rehearsal date from the date a file was copied; fourth, how to retain attributed source notes; fifth, an order for later digitization of the cassettes that does not assume their contents or condition. don't tell the writer to listen to every recording as the first step, since that could take too long and there may be unclear or restricted material.

keep the final part in view too. the requested plan should end with a brief, practical next-step paragraph that says what the volunteers can begin during their next four-hour work period, while making clear that uncertain rights, unidentified people, and incomplete inventories remain unresolved until checked. don't make that closing paragraph a claim that the archive is ready to publish, and don't add an imagined decision by the orchestra or its former players. keep all the details above, including the exact remarks and the access condition, in the organized prompt.
payload.response:
Write an internal cataloging and access plan for the North Stair Rehearsal Archive, a fictional community orchestra archive based in a former school music room in a port neighborhood. The archive holds rehearsal recordings from 2008 through 2022: mostly amateur digital files, a smaller group of MiniDiscs, and twelve cassette tapes that have not been digitized. The orchestra rehearsed weekly during the season, though some years have gaps because the room was closed for repairs. Do not portray the archive as larger or more complete than these facts support. The requested work is an internal plan, not a history or public announcement.

The plan is for two volunteer archivists who have about four hours a week between them, one shared laptop, and no dedicated server. The existing folder structure was created by different people over time, and dates and ensemble names are inconsistent. The main folder contains 186 digital audio files, including duplicates and a few exports without an original file alongside them. Two old external drives hold another 41 files, whose contents have not been checked against the main folder. Twelve cassettes are in paper sleeves, and only seven have handwritten dates. Do not imply that the material has already been listened to or inventoried unless stated here.

Use these collection details when making practical recommendations: the orchestra usually had 18 to 26 players, and a rehearsal could involve a full ensemble, a woodwind group, or a smaller string section. Reliable attendance sheets do not exist. Some filenames begin with a date, others use a piece title, and some say things like “final take” without identifying the recording. The conductor’s name appears on programs, but programs survive for only about half the years. A folder marked “old concert things” contains 9 programs, and nobody knows whether the folder is complete. Do not treat those programs as proof of who attended a particular rehearsal.

Make the plan usable without turning it into a software shopping list or a promise to process everything. Include a simple filename approach, a compact set of metadata fields, a cautious way to identify likely duplicates, and a manageable sequence of work. Fit the recommendations to the volunteers’ limited time and equipment. Do not claim that file checksums, transcription, or audio cleanup are already happening. Separate tasks they can undertake now from work requiring more time or expertise. Do not decide which recordings are musically important or rank performances. Do not prescribe a particular database or platform.

Retain the following remarks exactly, identifying each as an attributed source note rather than a verified catalog fact:

- The handwritten note on one MiniDisc says, “Nov 2014? winds, second half maybe.”
- A paper sleeve on cassette 3 says, “Mira says this is the winter concert run-through, not sure which year.”
- An email from a former player, received with the drive, says, “I think the room microphones were moved after the boiler work, but I can’t remember when.”

Explain how the plan can record these notes with their sources identified, without silently resolving uncertain dates, group types, or equipment history. Keep the wording and uncertainty in each remark exactly as written.

Address access separately from internal cataloging. For recordings made after 2018, consent forms exist for some sessions, but the archive has not matched every form to a recording. One former player has asked that their voice not be placed online, and the archivists do not yet know which files include that player. If a session’s consent form cannot be matched, hold that session back from online sharing while allowing internal preservation work to continue. If the player can be identified in a recording, do not propose publishing that file until the request is reviewed with them. payload.instruction:
MODE: /polish
LANGUAGE: en
PROFILE: Clear and professional.
INPUT:
The Ridgeway Climbing Club completed its spring gear inspection on May 14 at the north equipment room of the Alder Street climbing wall. The inspection covered club-owned equipment assigned to the adult lead, top-rope, and youth programs. Mara Chen coordinated the work, with Luis Ortega and Priya Nair recording observations. The team used the current inventory register and the manufacturers’ care instructions supplied with each equipment type. The room was dry, the overhead lights were working, and the inspection table had enough space to lay out each item without stacking it on other gear. No climbing session took place during the inspection.

Before handling the equipment, the inspectors confirmed that the register listed 42 harnesses, 31 ropes, 58 carabiners, 16 belay devices, and 12 helmets. They checked the item count against the shelves and marked each item with a temporary paper tag as it was examined. Harnesses and helmets were arranged by program, while ropes were laid out in separate lanes to avoid crossing their ends. The team kept the original labels visible and did not remove any manufacturer tags. A small number of items had handwritten notes from earlier routine checks; those notes were copied into the inspection log rather than treated as current findings.

The inspection used visual and hand checks appropriate to the equipment. Inspectors looked for cuts, abrasion, deformation, corrosion, contamination, damaged stitching, and unreadable labels. They operated each carabiner gate and checked that it closed without being held. Belay devices were examined for wear at contact points, and helmets were checked around the shell, suspension, and adjustment system. Ropes were inspected along their accessible lengths while being fed through the hands at a steady pace. The team did not perform destructive testing, remove sewn components, or make judgments about equipment that was not available for examination. Each observation was recorded with the item’s register number, location, and the initials of the inspector who entered it.

1. The harness count matched the register. The team examined waist belts, leg loops, tie-in points, buckles, and visible stitching on all 42 harnesses. Four items had small areas of surface dirt, but no cut webbing or separated stitching was recorded. The serial labels on harnesses H-018 and H-027 were difficult to read under the room lighting, so the inspectors used a handheld lamp and recorded the numbers that could be confirmed. Harness H-031 had a handwritten note dated February 3 describing a buckle adjustment; the present inspection found the buckle threaded correctly, and the old note remained in the log as historical information.

2. All 31 ropes were present. Each rope was checked for visible sheath damage, glazing, flat spots, contamination, and changes in diameter that could be detected by hand. Rope R-12 had a faded identification marking near one end, although its inventory number remained legible on the attached label. Rope R-19 had a short section with a noticeably rougher feel than the adjacent length. The inspectors marked that location with a loose paper tag and recorded its distance from the blue end. They did not cut the rope or attempt to determine the cause during this inspection. The remaining ropes had no specific surface observations entered in the log.

3. The carabiner count and belay-device count also matched the register. Each carabiner was checked for a smooth gate action, visible cracks, deformation, and corrosion. On carabiner C-044, the gate returned more slowly than on the other units, but it closed when released during the check. Carabiner C-051 had a shallow scratch on the spine with no visible distortion. The inspectors wrote, “Gate return was slower than the comparison units,” beside C-044’s number. All 16 belay devices were examined at their rope-contact surfaces; device D-006 showed a polished area, which was photographed beside a ruler for scale. The photograph was stored with the inspection record, not used as a measurement of remaining service life.

The 12 helmets were checked for visible shell damage, loose components, strap wear, and function of the adjustment systems. Helmet M-009 had a scuff on the left side, and the shell showed no crack under the available light. The adjustment dial on M-011 moved through its range during the hand check, though the inspectors noted that its action felt stiffer than the other dials. No helmet was dismantled. The team recorded the model and serial information wherever it was readable and flagged labels that could not be confirmed without better light. Priya noted, “Let’s keep the label question separate from the condition check,” and the log uses separate columns for identification and observed condition.

The inspection record distinguishes an observation from a disposition. The team did not mark equipment as approved for use, removed from service, or repaired on the basis of this inspection alone. Any later change in status is to be entered as a separate dated record by the club’s equipment coordinator. In particular, the rough-feeling section on R-19 remains an observation pending a closer review. If the follow-up examination is performed in a different room, the reviewer should use adequate lighting and record whether the same section still feels different from the surrounding rope. The inspection log does not state what that examination will find.

The paper tags were removed after their details had been transcribed, except for the tag marking the location on R-19, which was retained with the inspection folder so the location could be found again. Photographs were taken of C-044, D-006, and the two labels that were hard to read. The original files carry the date and item number in their filenames. No photograph was taken of an item when the written record already captured the relevant observation clearly. The team returned the equipment to its assigned shelves, keeping the three groups of gear separate as they had been before the inspection. The count was checked once more against the register before the equipment room was locked.

The inspection folder contains the signed attendance sheet, the marked inventory register, the observation log, and the referenced photographs. The summary file is stored alongside those records under its supplied filename:
delivery-summary.tsv
Mara’s final entry states, “The counts are complete, and the observations are recorded against the register numbers.” The club’s next equipment review is listed for August 20, but that date does not replace any item-specific follow-up noted in the log. Until a later dated entry is made, the recorded observations remain the full account of what the team saw and checked on May 14. The folder also notes that the original care instructions are kept in the cabinet beside the equipment-room door, available to the person carrying out any subsequent review.

MODE: /polish
LANGUAGE: pt
PROFILE: Friendly and conversational.

na terça-feira, a equipe da padaria Pão da Vila estava ajustando o formulário de encomendas para a semana de abertura do balcão novo. o formulário antigo deixava misturado o nome de quem fazia o pedido com o nome da pessoa que ia buscar, e isso tinha dado confusão em duas encomendas recentes. a gerente, Marta, pediu um campo para cada nome, mais telefone de contato e uma opção para a pessoa marcar se preferia receber mensagem ou ligação. ela não queria que o formulário prometesse confirmação automática: o pedido só ficava confirmado depois de alguém da equipe verificar disponibilidade e responder ao cliente.

O formulário novo ia ser usado para bolos, pães e caixas de doces, mas a equipe não queria transformar cada encomenda numa conversa longa. Por isso, os tamanhos dos bolos apareciam em opções separadas, com o diâmetro escrito em centímetros e o número de porções indicado como estimativa. Um bolo redondo de 20 centímetros era apresentado como suficiente para cerca de 10 porções; o de 26 centímetros, para cerca de 18. Marta pediu que a palavra “cerca” continuasse visível, porque a quantidade servia de orientação e não era uma garantia exata. Para bolos retangulares, o formulário pedia que a pessoa escrevesse as dimensões desejadas, em vez de escolher um tamanho que a padaria não oferecia sempre.

A encomenda que a equipe usou para testar os campos era da cliente Elisa Nunes. Ela solicitou 2 bolos de cenoura de 20 centímetros, e esse número era a quantidade de bolos, não o tamanho. Cada bolo tinha o diâmetro de 20 centímetros e uma estimativa de 10 porções. Ela também pediu 24 pãezinhos de queijo, que deveriam ser contados por unidade, e 3 caixas de seis brigadeiros, em que seis indicava os doces por caixa e três indicava o número de caixas. A equipe queria que as unidades aparecessem junto dos números para ninguém ler 24 como o peso dos pãezinhos ou seis como a quantidade total de caixas.

Marta explicou a escolha do campo de retirada assim: “se a pessoa marca retirada, a gente precisa saber o dia e a faixa de horário antes de aceitar o pedido”. No teste, Elisa escolheu quinta-feira, entre 15h e 16h, e indicou a loja da Rua das Palmeiras como local de retirada. A equipe não devia tratar a escolha do horário como confirmação. Se a padaria não conseguisse atender aquela faixa, alguém deveria entrar em contato com Elisa antes de mudar o horário ou sugerir outro. A opção de entrega ficava no mesmo formulário, mas só podia ser selecionada para endereços dentro do bairro Jardim Novo; para um endereço fora desse bairro, a equipe precisava combinar a retirada, sem marcar entrega como disponível.

1. Na parte de personalização, o formulário perguntava se havia uma mensagem no bolo, e limitava a mensagem a 30 caracteres, contando os espaços. Elisa escreveu “parabéns, vó Lúcia”, que tinha que ficar exatamente com essa grafia e esse acento, sem a equipe trocar a frase por uma versão mais curta. O campo seguinte perguntava sobre alergias ou ingredientes que a pessoa queria evitar. Elisa informou que a irmã tinha alergia a amendoim. Isso precisava ficar como informação recebida do cliente, não como confirmação de que todos os produtos da padaria eram livres de contato com amendoim.

A equipe queria uma nota clara perto desse campo para explicar que a observação seria repassada a quem preparasse o pedido, mas que a padaria não garantia ausência de contato cruzado na cozinha. Se um cliente informasse uma alergia grave, a encomenda teria de ser conversada com a gerente antes de ser aceita; o formulário, por si só, não aprovava nem recusava o pedido. Para Elisa, Marta anotou que a equipe deveria confirmar com ela os detalhes da alergia antes de finalizar a encomenda. Essa conversa ainda não tinha acontecido quando o teste foi registrado.

No painel interno, os pedidos para o balcão novo apareciam com uma etiqueta azul, mas o botão de impressão não devia alterar o estado da encomenda. A pessoa responsável pelo balcão precisava conferir primeiro o nome do cliente, a quantidade de cada item, o dia escolhido e se o pagamento estava registrado. A equipe usava “pendente” até essa conferência e só mudava para “confirmado” depois de responder ao cliente. Para testar a iluminação da placa do balcão ao lado da área de retirada, a equipe pediu que Rui abrisse este arquivo antes de ativar os sinais de luz:
lighting-cues.yaml

No formulário, a caixa para informar um código promocional era opcional, e a ausência de código não devia impedir o envio de um pedido. A equipe também decidiu não exibir um preço total antes de confirmar os itens personalizados e a disponibilidade do horário, porque o valor dos bolos com mensagem dependia do tamanho e da decoração solicitada. O formulário podia mostrar os preços unitários já definidos para os pãezinhos e para as caixas de brigadeiros. Esses preços não substituíam a confirmação final do valor da encomenda. Marta pediu que o aviso aparecesse antes do botão de envio, e não escondido no rodapé.

Na revisão seguinte, a equipe compararia o pedido de Elisa com a folha usada na cozinha: dois bolos, vinte e quatro unidades de pão de queijo, três caixas com seis brigadeiros cada, retirada na quinta-feira das 15h às 16h e mensagem de 30 caracteres no máximo. A equipe também deixaria visíveis o nome de quem buscaria, o telefone e a preferência de contato, mesmo que quem fizesse o pedido fosse outra pessoa. Se Elisa pedisse uma alteração depois das 16h de terça-feira, a padaria não devia substituir automaticamente os itens nem presumir que a nova solicitação cabia no horário escolhido; alguém teria de verificar de novo a disponibilidade e falar com ela. O formulário devia guardar essa solicitação como pendente até a resposta da equipe.

payload.instruction:
MODE: /prompt
LANGUAGE: en
INPUT:
Write a practical delivery and setup plan for the fictional Cedar Lane Sunday Market, focusing on the arrival of supplies for the stall called Orchard Jar. The plan is for the stall team and delivery driver to use on market morning, so make the sequence easy to follow under time pressure. Keep the distinction between confirmed details and matters that still need checking. Do not assume that a vehicle has access to the market square just because the stall is located there.

Orchard Jar sells small-batch preserves, chutneys, and gift boxes. The stall is run by Mara Ellis and her brother Tom; Mara handles the order sheets and customer display, while Tom normally unloads the vehicle and sets up the folding tables. Their market space is B-14, along the west row beside the flower seller. The Sunday market opens to customers at 9:00 a.m., and the stall team has permission to set up from 6:30 a.m. The delivery is planned for that morning, not the night before. The produce will come from their rented kitchen on Bell Street, about two miles from the market entrance, in a refrigerated van driven by Leon Price.

The order consists of 24 jars of plum jam, 18 jars of apple butter, 12 jars of pear chutney, and 10 gift boxes containing one jar of each preserve. The jars are sealed and labeled, but the boxes are packed separately so that they can be arranged without crushing the labels. There are also two crates of tasting spoons, a small signboard, a cash box, paper bags, and a roll of compostable table covering. The preserve cartons must remain upright. The gift boxes should not be stacked beneath the jars, and the tasting spoons and cash box should stay with Mara rather than being left beside the unloading area. Include these distinctions in the handling sequence instead of treating all items as interchangeable cargo.

The van is booked to leave the kitchen at 6:40 a.m. Leon expects the drive to take 15 to 20 minutes if Bell Street traffic is light, but he has not checked whether the market’s morning road closure affects the final approach. The usual public entrance is on Cedar Lane, where vehicles are prohibited between 7:00 and 9:00 a.m. On the previous Sunday, a delivery driver was directed to the loading gate on Mill Court. That recollection is useful but is not confirmation that the gate will be open this week. Ask the plan to identify the person responsible for checking the current access instructions before departure, and to state what information should be confirmed with the market office.

Mara said, “If the Mill Court gate is open, we can unload beside the west row; if it is locked, we need the service-lane instructions before Leon turns into Cedar Lane.” Treat that as a genuine condition for choosing the approach, not as confirmation that either route is available. The service lane is narrow, and the van cannot pass a parked car there. If the market office directs Leon to use it, the plan should account for checking that it is clear before the van enters and should avoid suggesting that the driver stop where the route would block other deliveries. Do not resolve the access question by inventing a gate code, a road-closure exception, or permission to unload at the public entrance.

Please organize the requested plan into the following numbered section, followed by a short set of practical notes for the team:
1. A pre-departure check at the kitchen, including the order count, chilled-van temperature reading, carton arrangement, contact numbers, and access confirmation.
2. The morning sequence from the van’s planned departure through arrival, unloading, and handoff of the items to Mara and Tom. Distinguish the planned times from estimates and identify the timing that depends on the market office’s reply.
3. A stall setup order for the cartons, gift boxes, signboard, table covering, and tasting supplies, with sensible attention to keeping customer-facing stock clean and labels visible.
4. A brief contingency branch for the two possible access outcomes described above. Make clear which facts are known, which require confirmation, and who should pause to ask for instructions if the gate status or route differs from expectations.

Tom has a folding hand truck with two usable wheels and a rated capacity of 80 kilograms, but the team has not weighed the packed crates. Do not calculate a total load or state that the hand truck can safely carry everything. Instead, include a check that the team should compare the actual load with the equipment rating and make separate trips if necessary. The market has uneven paving near the west row; mention careful movement and keeping the cartons upright, without claiming that a particular path is level or unobstructed. The van’s temperature display is readable from the driver’s seat, but the acceptable transport temperature for these preserves has not been supplied. Do not invent a temperature threshold; ask the team to use the kitchen’s handling instructions and record the reading for the person responsible for the goods.

Leon told Tom, “I can call when I leave Bell Street, but I may not have a safe place to stop once I’m near the market.” Reflect that limit in the communication sequence: use the departure call to share the estimated arrival, and do not make the plan depend on Leon reading or answering messages while driving. Mara will carry the current order sheet and has the market office number saved in her phone. Tom has the stall key and can contact Mara, but he does not have the office number. Make the roles clear so the driver is not left to settle a site-access dispute on his own.

The plan should be concise enough to consult on a phone, but detailed enough that a substitute stall assistant could follow the loading and setup sequence. Use plain language, a clear chronological order, and brief headings. Include the actual quantities and named locations supplied here; do not silently change them or add stock. Keep the distinction between the 6:30 setup permission, the 6:40 planned departure, the 9:00 customer opening, and the estimated drive time. Do not promise that delivery will be completed by a particular minute, since the access instructions and approach have not yet been confirmed.

End with a substantive final paragraph describing the handoff at the stall: Mara should check the delivered count against the order sheet, Tom should report any damaged or tilted cartons before stock is displayed, and the team should keep the tasting supplies and cash box under Mara’s control. Include the practical condition that if the confirmed route changes on arrival, Leon should wait in a safe permitted place and contact Mara for updated instructions rather than choosing an unverified entrance. Do not turn this into a claim that damage, delay, or a route change has occurred; it is a procedure for the delivery team to use if needed.

Two society members will set up the welcome table and the sign-in sheets, and one volunteer will stay near the main entrance to direct guests to the accessible route. The old side entrance is shorter, but it has two steps, so it cannot be the route listed on the event page. We should also bring a small lamp for the table, since the overhead lights near the screen will be dimmed before the screening starts. I wrote down that we need tape, extension cords, water cups, and the printed guides. I nearly wrote paper plates there, but we do not need those.

The rights office has not given us a fee yet, so leave that line blank in the budget rather than guessing.
