Mara: quick update on the ceramics delivery for the north gallery. the carrier has us down for thursday, 9:30–11:00, at the service entrance on Bell Street. there are 18 cartons total, including the two display plinths, and the driver needs the receiving bay kept clear for about 20 minutes.

Dev: i checked the order against the packing list this morning. it’s 12 dinner plates, 8 serving bowls, 6 handled mugs, and 4 small vases, plus the plinths. the plates are the ash-white run, not the earlier cream sample, so please use the updated shelf labels when we count them.

Mara: the studio sent a photo from the final inspection. Their note says, "The blue glaze is darker in person, but the rim is clean." I’ve saved it in the delivery folder beside the invoice and the carton map. that should help if anyone asks about the shade at intake.

Luis: one useful detail from the packing sheet: Packing note: "Keep the two repaired bowls upright; the handles face inward." they’re in carton 7, with the tissue wrap marked in orange. don't stack the sample tiles on top of that carton, even if there looks like room in the van.

Nia: i can meet the driver, but i have a school pickup at 11:15, so i can’t stay late if the slot slips. Could someone from the gallery team be the backup contact? the driver’s number ends in 2841, and they asked us not to call before 8:00 unless the route changes.

Dev: I’ll be there by 9:15 to move the folding table and put the trolley near the ramp. the ramp is usable, but the right wheel catches on the metal strip, so we should pull the trolley rather than push it down. Facilities said they can’t fix that before Friday.

Mara: a couple of checks before Thursday:
1. count all 18 cartons against the map before signing the delivery slip.
2. photograph any crushed corners while the cartons are still on the truck.
3. compare the two repaired bowls with the inspection photo, but leave the wrapping on until the conservator arrives.
4. put the ash-white plates on the lower shelf, where the old cream sample used to sit.

Luis: the forecast shows showers from late morning, and the service entrance awning only covers the first half of the bay. If rain starts before 10:00, we should ask the driver to unload under the covered loading dock around the corner, then wheel everything through the west corridor. I’ll bring the waterproof crate covers just in case.

Nia: small correction to the dock plan, the west corridor is booked for a lighting delivery until 10:30. If we use the loading dock, we need to wait until that crew clears the corridor, unless they finish early and facilities confirms the route is open. the freight lift is free, but it fits only one trolley at a time.

Dev: good catch. I’ll ask facilities to confirm by 8:45, not assume the corridor is clear. If rain starts before 10:00 and the corridor is still blocked, we can hold the cartons under the dock cover and keep them on the truck if the driver agrees. we shouldn't move them through the public lobby.

Mara: the driver said on the phone, "I can wait ten minutes at the dock, but I can’t leave the truck unattended." I wrote that down in the delivery folder too. That means we’ll need someone at the bay while another person checks the corridor, rather than sending everyone upstairs to clear space.

Luis: I’ve asked Omar from facilities to be the second person. He can check the corridor and unlock the freight lift, but he’s covering two buildings, so he may arrive closer to 10. the loading dock is on Quarry Lane, not the alley behind the gallery; the map pin in the old email is wrong.

Nia: thanks, I’ll update the shared calendar with Quarry Lane and the new contact plan. I also found three empty padded bins in storage, which should be enough for the loose tile samples. the bins are labeled “fragile—studio return,” so let’s leave those labels on until the samples are unpacked and logged.

Dev: for the intake paperwork, the invoice lists the replacement value as $2,460, while the carrier sheet shows $2,640. I’ve emailed the studio to confirm which figure belongs on our receipt, and we should leave that field blank until they reply. everything else on the invoice matches the order number, CG-418.

Mara: the gallery opens at noon, and the opening team needs the main aisle by 11:30. If the delivery is still being unloaded at 11:00, we’ll keep the plinths in the receiving bay and bring the smaller cartons through first, as long as the west corridor is open. Don’t put anything in front of the fire panel.

Luis: I can stay until 11:40, but after that I’m due at the kiln room across town. I’ll bring the hand truck, two blankets, and a roll of floor protection; the gallery’s spare hand truck has a loose strap. please message me if the carrier changes the time, since i won’t see updates while I’m driving.

Nia: I’ll take the 9:00 check-in and text the group when I’m at the service entrance. If the truck hasn’t arrived by 10:45, I’ll call the number ending in 2841, then let Mara know before I sign anything. I can stay for the first count, but I can’t be the only person handling the paperwork.

Mara: final note for Thursday: keep the invoice question open, use the corrected Quarry Lane pin, and don’t unwrap the repaired bowls before the conservator arrives. On rainy days it can take longer, which is another reason I’d rather not ask for a lesson that begins right at four.

I can sometimes make Wednesdays work, but that depends on Luis’s work schedule, and I don’t want to say yes to a Wednesday slot until I’ve checked with him. We are not asking for a trial lesson with a different teacher; Mateo would like to work with Jo because he heard her play at the studio’s spring student concert.

There are a few details that may help with the booking. Mateo’s full name is Mateo Ruiz, and his birthday is February 8, 2013. My best contact number is the one already on the family account, ending in 4826; email is also fine for schedule questions. If the studio needs a separate emergency contact, use Luis Ruiz at the number ending in 9173. Please list me as the parent who requested the lesson, even though Luis may be the one who brings Mateo on Tuesdays. If a form asks who will usually attend, the answer is Mateo, with either parent dropping him off and picking him up.

1. We can bring a notebook, pencil, and the beginner piano book Mateo already has, if Jo is happy to use it. The book is called First Steps at the Piano, by Nora Bell, and it is the blue edition. I’m not asking the studio to order another copy. Mateo’s school teacher recommended that he keep a practice log, so we can bring that too, though it is only a sheet in a folder and not a formal book.
2. Our piano at home is an upright with 88 keys, and it is tuned, although the low A has started to sound a little dull. Mateo can practice there, but he does not have a keyboard to bring to lessons. I’m mentioning the low note in case Jo asks what kind of instrument he uses; it is not a request for the studio to arrange a repair or assess the piano.
3. We have read the studio’s usual cancellation note. If Mateo is ill, I’ll contact the studio as soon as I can rather than bring him in. I understand that the studio may have its own notice period, but I couldn’t tell from the page whether a missed lesson can be made up. Please send me the current policy or point me to the right page; I’m not asking you to promise a makeup lesson.
4. Luis asked whether the first payment is due when the lesson is booked or at the first visit. I don’t know which way the studio handles it, so please let me know the amount and due date once you confirm the schedule. We can pay by card or check, and I don’t need you to charge anything before we know which time is available.

One calendar complication is that Mateo’s school is closed for fall break on Tuesday, October 22. If Jo’s Tuesday time is available and the booking starts on October 15, please leave October 22 out and have the next lesson be October 29; we will be out of town that week and cannot attend remotely. I don’t want that week moved to Wednesday or counted as a request for an extra lesson. If the regular weekly start would instead be later than October 15, let me know what date you have in mind before applying the fall-break note, because the October 22 detail only matters if Mateo is already scheduled to begin before then.

Jo told Mateo after the spring concert, “We can start with short pieces and build up from there,” and he came home excited about choosing music with her. I’m not expecting him to learn a particular song right away, and I haven’t promised him a performance date. He does enjoy film music and simple tunes he can recognize, so that may be useful background for Jo, but I’d rather let her decide what is appropriate for a first lesson. Could you pass that along when you send her the booking request? If she needs any more information about his playing level or the book, I can answer by email. For now, the main request is the Tuesday 4:30 weekly time with Jo, with a check-in from you first if it is unavailable, and the October 22 exception only if the start date makes it relevant.

INPUT:
i'm Tessa, the workshop coordinator at North Quay Makers, and i did the ventilation check in the metal room on Tuesday morning, 14 May. The room had been open for about twenty minutes before i started, and the outside temperature was 12 degrees. We were checking the fixed extraction hood and the two flexible arms before a scheduled evening class, not doing a full building inspection. I used the checklist from the maintenance folder, but wrote the readings on a separate sheet because the printed boxes are too small for the meter numbers. The check took a little over an hour, with pauses while people moved equipment out of the way.

Malik, our technician, removed the mesh pre-filter from the fixed hood, washed it, and put it back after it had dried. He also checked the flexible arm joints and tightened the loose clamp on the arm nearest the bench grinder. I didn't remove either arm or adjust the fan controls. Malik told me the clamp had been loose for a while, but he couldn't say when it first became that way. He left the removed filter on the drying rack while we took the first readings, so the hood reading from that part of the check is not a reading with the filter installed. We put the filter back before taking the later readings.

I used the same handheld airflow meter throughout and recorded the display in metres per second. At the fixed hood, the first reading with the filter off was 5.1. With the filter back in place, the three readings were 4.6, 4.5, and 4.6. At the grinder arm, the readings after Malik tightened the clamp were 3.2, 3.3, and 3.2. At the second arm, beside the welding table, I got 2.8, 2.9, and 2.8. I wrote down the range as well as each individual number, because the display moved a little while I was holding the meter at the opening.

The readings were taken with the workshop's large roller door shut and the pedestrian door closed, although people did open the pedestrian door between sets to carry through a cart. I waited until it was shut again before starting each set. The portable fan by the paint cupboard was switched off, and the ceiling lights were on. I did not check the dust collector, the paint cupboard, or the small soldering bench, since those were outside the scope of this check. There was some grinding noise from the next room, but no one was using the grinder in our room during the measurements.

1. The fixed hood was clear of stored items, but a box of spare gloves sat on the shelf below it. The box did not cover the hood opening. I moved a stool that had been parked in front of the grinder arm, then took the measurements with the arm pulled out to the usual working position, around 35 centimetres above the bench.
2. Malik checked the date sticker on the meter and said it was due for its next service in September. I copied the serial number from the back of the meter onto my sheet, but I have not checked that number against the service log yet.
3. There was a strip of grey tape on the floor marking where the welding table usually sits. The table was about half a metre farther from the wall than the strip during the check, because a new storage cabinet had been delivered the day before. I did not move the table, and I took the arm readings in its current position.
4. The door closer on the pedestrian door worked, but the door took a few seconds to latch after it was released. I noted that because it was opened a few times during the hour, and I wanted the sheet to show the room conditions rather than suggest the door stayed closed without interruption.

i'm writing about a preference for PagePin, the browser extension our small research group uses to save articles and notes. the preference i want to discuss is whether the capture panel stays open after a page is saved. right now, PagePin closes the panel after each save, which is fine when someone is collecting one link, but less handy when they are clipping several sources from the same report. i'm not asking for the panel to stay open for everybody automatically. i'd like Luis, who maintains the extension, to consider adding a setting so each person can choose what happens next.

for context, we use PagePin in Chrome on the shared lab laptops and on our own computers. the extension saves the page title, address, capture time, and any note typed into the panel. it does not save the page itself, and i don't want this request to sound like a change to what information gets collected. the panel currently has a title field, a note box, a collection menu, and a blue Save button. after a save, the panel disappears and the small PagePin icon shows the saved count. that behavior is simple to understand, even if it interrupts a longer batch of captures.

last Tuesday, my colleague Theo tried a sequence of article captures while preparing the coastal-planning packet. he saved a city report, opened a second tab, and then opened the PagePin panel again to save a university brief. he repeated that cycle for seven pages. Theo did the test on his own laptop, not on a shared machine, and he was using the current public version of Chrome. he told me, “I keep reopening the same little panel, and it breaks my place in the reading.” that was his description of the task, not a claim that PagePin lost any of his notes. i watched him finish the packet, but i did not count how much time the repeated openings took.

Theo also tried pinning the panel from Chrome's toolbar. that kept the toolbar visible, but it did not keep PagePin's capture panel open after he pressed Save. he later switched back to the ordinary panel because the pinned view took space from the article. i haven't checked whether Chrome behaves the same way on every operating system, and i don't know if the extension can tell which panel layout a person is using. those details may matter to Luis when he looks at the request, so i want to keep them as questions rather than assume an answer.

my request to Luis is to consider a small preference called something like “Keep the capture panel open after saving.” i'm not attached to that exact label. the setting could be in PagePin's options page, near the existing choice for the default collection, rather than appearing as another control inside every capture. if Luis thinks the options page is not the right place, i'm open to a different location. the important part for me is that this is an individual preference and that the existing close-after-save behavior can still be selected.

there are a few details that might make the request easier to review:
1. the preference should let a person choose whether Save closes the panel or leaves it open for another capture; it should not change the saved title, address, capture time, or note.
2. when the panel remains open, the current page's saved information should not appear as if it were a new unsaved capture. the person would need to be able to move to another page and start a separate capture in the usual way.
3. the collection menu should continue to show the collection selected for the next save, rather than silently switching to a different collection. if PagePin already refreshes that menu as a person changes collections, this request isn't asking to alter that rule.
4. the preference should be easy to reverse, so a person who tries it can return to automatic closing without reinstalling the extension or losing their saved items.

these are the behaviors i have in mind, not a claim about how the extension is built today. i haven't inspected PagePin's code, and i don't know whether the panel can reset its fields after a save without closing. i would rather Luis decide whether that is practical than suggest a technical implementation that might not fit the extension. i can share the coastal-planning example with him if it helps, but i haven't sent him Theo's notes or asked Theo to file a separate issue.

there is also a condition that matters for how this could be used: if someone is working on a shared lab laptop, they should be able to leave the setting off and keep the current close-after-save behavior. i don't want a choice made on my own computer to change the experience for everyone who uses a lab laptop. i assume the preference would belong to the browser profile, but i haven't confirmed how PagePin stores its existing options, so that part needs checking rather than being treated as settled. Theo did his captures on his own laptop; he didn't change any preference on the shared machines.

Maya, our project coordinator, asked me to put the request in writing before the next planning meeting, and Luis is the person i am asking to review it. Maya did not ask Luis to build the setting, and i have not told the group that it will be included. i can send Luis the approximate date of Theo's test and the Chrome version if he needs them; i have not recorded the exact version number yet. the packet included a city transportation report, a university brief, two maps, and several policy pages, so the repeated capture flow came up while moving among different kinds of sources, not just near-identical web pages.

i'd also like to be clear about what would count as a useful discussion with Luis. he could tell me whether a per-profile preference is feasible, ask for details about the panel behavior, or suggest a different way to handle a run of captures. i'm asking him to consider the setting, not requesting that he promise a release date or say the feature is approved. if the panel cannot stay open without causing another problem, i would want to hear what constraint he found before we talk about alternatives. i can describe what Theo did, but i can't speak for how every member of the group would choose to use the preference.

for the next planning meeting, i'll bring the current PagePin screen description, Theo's account of reopening the panel seven times, and the condition about keeping shared laptop profiles independent from my own. the meeting is scheduled for Thursday afternoon in the small conference room, and Maya asked me to send Luis the written request beforehand so he has time to look at it. i have not yet sent it. the request should remain focused on the panel after saving, with the saved information and collection behavior staying as they are, unless Luis identifies a technical detail that needs a separate conversation.

we have been using one shared meal calendar for the family since september, and it is meant to show dinners, who is cooking, and anything that changes what people can eat. It is not a plan that everyone has to follow exactly. I usually find it helpful when the entries are settled by sunday evening, because then I can do the grocery list on monday morning, but that timing is my preference and not a rule for everybody. The calendar is in the family folder, and the paper copy is on the refrigerator beside the school notices. Dad updates the paper one, while I keep the shared version on my phone, so sometimes the two do not match for a few hours.

The current week begins on Monday, the 14th, and ends on Sunday, the 20th. Monday is lentil soup with bread, and I have put a note that the soup should be made mild because Noah does not like much pepper. Tuesday is the leftover rice night, with eggs or vegetables added if there is enough for the people who are home. On Wednesday, Lena is bringing the spinach pie from the bakery near the library. She said, “I can pick it up after work, but I cannot promise I will be home before six.” I have therefore left the serving time open instead of putting down six o’clock as if it were definite.

Thursday is still marked as chicken and roasted carrots, but that entry depends on whether Mayra confirms her work shift by Thursday morning. If she is working late, she will not be able to stop at the market, and we may need to use the frozen fish already in the freezer instead. The fish is enough for four, not six, so if Mayra's shift runs late and all six of us are eating, I will need to ask Dad to pick up another main dish on his way home. This is one reason the calendar should show the condition and not just say “chicken” in a way that looks final. Mayra has not confirmed yet, so the chicken is not a settled meal.

Friday has been left open because the children may eat at school after the concert rehearsal. That is not confirmed either, and the school has not sent the final rehearsal time. If they do eat at school, there will still be three adults at home, and we can heat the extra soup or make sandwiches. If they come home for dinner, I would rather use the baked potatoes that are already in the pantry, with cheese and beans, instead of starting a different meal late. Dad said, “Please don’t count the rehearsal as dinner until the school sends the time.” I put that reminder in the calendar notes, not in the meal name.

Saturday is my turn to cook, and I am planning pasta with tomato sauce and a green salad. The sauce is from the batch I made last month and froze in two containers; one container should be enough for five, although it may be slightly short if everyone wants seconds. I can add the small jar of sauce in the cupboard, but that jar is spicy, so I do not want it mixed in before Noah has his portion. The salad can be made with lettuce, cucumber, and the last few radishes, if they are still good when I check them on Saturday. I wrote “check radishes” on the shopping list rather than assuming they will be usable.

Sunday is marked for soup and toast, using whatever vegetables need to be used before the next grocery trip. That is a flexible plan, not a promise to use every leftover. A few things in the fridge belong to other meals: the yogurt is for breakfasts, and the cooked beans are for Tuesday, unless Tuesday changes. If we use the beans on another day, the calendar should be updated so I do not buy more for no reason. I occasionally find that leftover notes are confusing when they are written as if something has already been served, so I am trying to mark them as planned until we actually use them.

1. For each dinner, the calendar should include the meal, the person responsible, and a short note only when it affects shopping or preparation. It does not need a full recipe. The lentil soup needs the mild-pepper note; Saturday’s pasta needs the reminder about keeping some sauce separate; and Thursday needs the work-shift condition. For a meal with no special detail, the meal name is enough. I think this keeps the page readable, although perhaps the paper copy could use a small symbol for meals that are not confirmed yet. We have not chosen a symbol, so for now the word “pending” is clearer.

2. The shopping list is separate from the calendar, but the two should be checked together. At present, we need bread, eggs, lettuce, cucumber, and possibly another main dish for Thursday. We do not need lentils, pasta, or canned beans because those are already in the cupboard. The cheese amount is uncertain: there is some in the fridge, but I have not checked whether it will cover the potatoes and the lunch sandwiches. Add cheese only after checking the package, rather than buying another block automatically. If the children eat at school on Friday, the potatoes can stay in the pantry for another night; if they come home, use them Friday as planned.

Dad prefers the paper copy because he can see it when he opens the refrigerator, while Lena and I use the phone version when we are away from home. I do not think we need to force everybody onto one method. The practical issue is that changes made on paper do not appear on the phone unless I enter them, and sometimes I only notice the change when I am already making the shopping list. Dad agreed to tell me when he changes a meal, and I will update the shared calendar when I see his note. That may not happen immediately, especially on mornings when I leave early, so the date on the latest update matters more than trying to make the two copies change at the same moment.

I have left the following week mostly blank because we have not checked everyone’s schedule yet. The only entry there is Tuesday, when Lena expects to bring back the casserole dish, not a meal assignment. She said, “I’ll know my late shifts after the manager posts the rota.” Once she knows, we can place her cooking night on an evening when she is home in time. Until then, her name should not be attached to a dinner just because Tuesday is the only line with a note. The new shopping list can wait until we have reviewed that week, since the current list is only for the 14th through the 20th and should not include groceries for meals that are still undecided.

we're getting ready for a small photo-importer pilot at the North Hall archive, and i need a useful engineering prompt out of these notes. the importer reads a manifest in order and turns eligible photo records into work for the upload service. one record corresponds to one image, with a source path, a capture date when known, and a stable archive identifier. don't design a new importer from scratch; ask for a focused proposal for how to use batches in the existing import flow. the archive team has about 18,000 records in its full collection, but the first pilot file is expected to be smaller, around 430 records. those figures are planning context, not batch-size requirements.

the helper we already have is below. include it as supplied context and ask the engineer to explain where it would fit, rather than silently replacing it or assuming it already handles every importer concern. keep the lines exactly as shown:
def batch_records(records, width=7):
    return [records[start:start + width] for start in range(0, len(records), width)]

there are two possible sources for the batch width. if the manifest contains a `batch_width` value that is an integer greater than zero, use that value for the import. otherwise, including when the value is absent, zero, negative, or not an integer, use the helper's default width of 7. don't reject the whole manifest just because that optional field is missing or invalid. i'd like the proposal to make this rule easy to see and to explain whether the existing helper needs a small adjustment to accept the chosen width. it should not imply that a valid custom width is ignored.

the importer already has a dry-run option used by collection staff before they start a real transfer. if dry-run is on, calculate and report the planned batches, but do not upload, move, or modify any image files. if dry-run is off, pass the batches into the existing upload flow. keep those branches distinct; dry-run is not a partial upload mode. there is also an import log with a job identifier and the number of eligible records, and the proposal should say what batch-level information would make a failed run understandable without suggesting that the importer should log image contents or private metadata.

please make the treatment of ordering and incomplete final batches explicit. Records should stay in manifest order, and the final batch can contain fewer records than the selected width. For example, 16 eligible records at width 7 would make batches of 7, 7, and 2; that's just an example for explaining the behavior, not a hard-coded special case. A manifest with no eligible records should produce no upload batches. Do not pad a short final batch with empty records, and don't reorder images to make batches look more even. The engineer should also mention how an empty input is reported in dry-run mode.

1. cover the proposal in a practical order: describe the current flow and the narrow change, state the width-selection rule, then explain dry-run versus real import behavior. Include a short test plan with ordinary cases such as the default width, a valid custom width, an invalid optional width, a short last batch, and an empty eligible set. Include a dry-run test that verifies no upload side effect occurs. We don't need a broad test strategy for unrelated upload, authentication, or image-processing features. Please distinguish what is already stated here from any implementation detail that still needs a decision; don't assume an API or storage layout that i haven't named.

our support lead put it this way: "I can tell which folder failed, but not which files were skipped." Please use that as a signal to consider useful, privacy-conscious batch logging, not as a request to include extra personal data. For a failed real import, the team would like enough information to identify the job, batch position, and record count, and to tell whether later batches were attempted. Don't claim that retries or rollback already exist. If you discuss either, label it as an open question rather than a current capability. The immediate request is about batching and observability, not a redesign of failure recovery.

the importer is used by a few staff members who run one collection at a time, and they need a proposal they can review before a developer changes the pilot branch. Mention that the full collection size is not a reason to load every record's image bytes into memory. The proposal can identify memory use as something to check, but don't invent a required streaming design or a performance target. It should be clear that the task is to recommend a small, reviewable integration and tests, not to write a complete production importer or perform the pilot.

one more thing for the later discussion: if resumable imports are considered in a future phase, stable batch identifiers may matter, but do not add resumability to this change or treat it as approved. For this proposal, say briefly what question would need answering before a resume feature could be specified, without deciding its behavior now. Keep the request grounded in the facts above, and end by asking for the proposal and tests in a format that a developer and the archive staff can both review.

we need a Python change, preferably a narrowly scoped patch with the helper and the point where it is used. there is a sketch from the discussion below; keep this supplied code material exactly as shown in the final request and use it as the starting point when describing the change:
def batch_records(records, width=24):
    return [records[start:start + width] for start in range(0, len(records), width)]

The default batch width should remain 24, and callers should be able to provide a different positive width when the importer has a reason to do so. Please say what should happen for a zero or negative width rather than letting the behavior be accidental; the expected behavior is to reject it clearly. A width of 1 is valid. The last batch may be smaller than the others, and the helper should not create an empty batch for an empty input. Do not change the record fields, read image bytes, add a database layer, or add a new user-facing setting as part of this patch. There are a couple of constraints about what counts as one import. A session is one user-selected import root, with its selected folders and manifest entries. The importer can run more than one session in a day, and a retry is still associated with its original session. Keep session boundaries intact: records from two roots must never be combined in the same batch, even if the first root ends with a short batch. Also, batching must not reorder the records. The manifest already has an order chosen by the existing scan, and that order is meaningful to the coordinators. Album keys are metadata, not a reason to sort or group records. The source note from the review is: “Keep the camera's original sequence when timestamps tie.” Please retain that note as written and let it inform the ordering requirement.

Filtering is already part of the importer flow, and the timing matters. The user can select a subset of the scanned records before processing begins. If a subset is selected, make batches from that selected sequence after the selection step, not from the full manifest before filtering. Otherwise the groups sent onward can include records the user did not choose. There is also a cancel point after selection and before dispatch; if the user cancels there, do not send any batches to the processing stage. This is an integration condition, not a request to change how the selection screen or cancellation UI works. Preserve the current selection behavior and make the new batching step respect it.

Mina said, “The importer should feel steady, not clever.” Theo said, “A folder can be retried without starting a new album.” Keep both remarks in the organized prompt as ordinary context, not as requirements for a particular interface design. The second remark is relevant to the session/retry boundary: a retry should not cause records from another import root to be appended to its batches. We meet every Wednesday in the Old Library seminar room, and we have twenty-three active members this term. The society has borrowed a folding screen from the language department and two powered speakers from the radio club. The volunteer has permission to photograph the audience area but not to record the film or the discussion, and that limit was repeated at the meeting.

I am forwarding the family meal calendar to everyone before Sunday because the paper copy on the refrigerator is hard to read from the kitchen doorway, and two people have asked which version is current. The calendar covers the first three weeks of October and includes dinner plans, shopping notes, and the names of whoever is cooking. I added the dates after checking the school newsletter and the community center schedule, so the late pickup on Thursday and the library meeting on the second Tuesday are already marked. Nobody needs to treat the calendar as a promise about exact serving times because those may shift when the bus is delayed.

The calendar is meant to help us share the work without making every meal a separate group discussion. On the first Sunday, we have lentil soup with bread and sliced pears. On Monday, the plan is rice with roasted vegetables and yogurt. On Tuesday, there is a choice between leftover soup and baked potatoes, depending on what is still in the refrigerator. Wednesday is listed as a takeout night because Aunt Mara will be at her evening class, and Thursday is chicken with green beans unless the grocery delivery arrives after six. Friday is open for people to use the eggs and vegetables left from the week, and Saturday has no meal written in because the cousins may visit, but nobody has confirmed that yet.

I kept the notes beside the days instead of putting them in a separate shopping document, so Dad can see that the soup needs two cans of white beans and the bread should be the unsliced loaf from the bakery near the post office. The pears are already in the fruit bowl, and they do not need to go on the list. There is also a reminder to set aside one portion of soup for Grandma before everybody serves themselves. She likes to take it home in the small blue container, and the lid for that container is in the drawer under the oven mitts. I checked that detail with her yesterday, and she said, “Please label mine because I can never tell the soup apart from the gravy.”

The numbered section at the bottom is there for the jobs that do not fit beside a particular dinner:
1. Mara will check the pantry shelf for lentils and rice before she leaves for class.
2. I can pick up the bread on Sunday afternoon if the bakery is open past three.
3. Dad can wash the green beans while the chicken is in the oven.
4. The person who gets home first on Monday can put the pears on the table.

These are suggestions for dividing the work, not assignments that anyone has already agreed to. I left the names in place because they help us start the conversation, and we can change a job in the family chat if a schedule turns out differently.

There are a few practical details that could otherwise get lost. The grocery delivery is booked for Thursday in a window between four and seven, and the driver has the side entrance code. The bags should go on the bench just inside that entrance rather than on the porch because the porch light is not working well this week. If the delivery has not arrived by six, then we should use the frozen chicken that is already in the lower freezer drawer and leave the fresh chicken for next week. I wrote that condition next to Thursday so nobody has to guess which package the note means. The green beans are in the crisper and need to be used soon.

For Monday, the rice is in the tall glass jar above the dishwasher, and the roasted vegetables can be whatever is left from the peppers, carrots, and squash in the lower refrigerator drawer. There is olive oil on the counter, but the small bottle is almost empty, and the larger bottle is on the shelf by the tea tin. Dad asked whether the yogurt was plain or vanilla, and I told him the calendar says plain because that is what goes with the vegetables. He said, “Good, then I will leave the honey where it is for breakfast.” That was a comment about the breakfast shelf and not an extra dinner item, so the meal notes do not need another line for honey.

I also wrote down the timing around the library meeting because it affects who can start dinner on the second Tuesday. Mara usually leaves the house at five forty, and the meeting begins at six fifteen at the east branch. She said she can put the potatoes in the oven before she goes if someone else is able to turn them once they have been in for twenty minutes. I have not put a name beside that part because I do not know who will be home then. The potatoes are in the basket beside the pantry, and there is a clean baking tray on the middle oven rack. Please let the person who takes that job know in the chat rather than changing the whole calendar.

The open spaces are intentional. There is no meal plan for Saturday because the cousins have not confirmed a visit, and there is no Sunday dinner written for the final weekend because Grandma may be staying with my sister by then. If the cousins confirm before Friday afternoon, then we can add a simple lunch for them and use the extra bread. Otherwise, the bread can go in the freezer for the following week. I have not bought anything for either possibility. The date at the top of the calendar is October first, and the last date shown is October twenty-first, so we can add another page later without squeezing more notes into the margins.

When you open the forwarded file, the first page should show the three weeks, and the numbered jobs should be visible underneath the dinner table on a phone screen. The color marks are only there to make the cook names easier to spot: blue means Dad, green means Mara, and orange means me. The unmarked meals are still open for discussion. I used the same colors as the paper calendar, but the file can be printed in black and white without losing the names. If anyone cannot open the attachment, tell me which device you are using, and I can send the plain text version instead.

I am forwarding the calendar now so everyone has the same dates and notes before the weekend. Please look especially at Thursday because the delivery condition changes what we should cook, and at Saturday because that plan depends on whether the cousins confirm. We can leave the other meals as written unless someone sees a date that conflicts with a class pickup or appointment. The small blue container is clean, the pantry notes are current, and the final weekend remains open for now.

This is my account of the ventilation check in the small repair workshop at Cedar Street on Tuesday morning. The main action is forwarding the inspection packet to the facilities desk before noon so they can use the notes when they plan the next service visit. I am forwarding the packet because the maintenance calendar is being set this week, and the desk asked for a record of what we actually checked. The packet has the room sketch, the fan labels, the reading sheet, and a short note from Mara at the front office. I checked that each page was in the folder before I left the workshop, and the original reading sheet stays in the blue binder by the tool cabinet.

We began at eight fifteen after the night shift had moved its carts away from the intake wall. The workshop was open, but no cutting or sanding was underway during the check. The east door was closed, and the high window above the sink was open about a hand width. I noted both details because the room does not behave the same way when the doors are left open. The wall fan is marked F2, and the ceiling extractor is marked E1. Those labels match the sketch from last autumn, although the tape on the extractor switch is peeling at the lower corner.

Mara unlocked the narrow electrical cupboard and waited while I checked the meter against the small reference unit from the stores shelf. The meter display came on without a warning symbol, and the reference unit was within its date for the check. I wrote down the serial numbers rather than relying on the labels because the label on the meter case has a crease through the final digit. The serial ending forty-eight belongs to the meter, and the unit ending eleven belongs to the reference device. I returned both units to Mara before we started taking readings. She kept the cupboard key on her ring throughout.

We took readings at the marked floor position near the centre bench and at the two pencil marks beside the paint rack. I used the same height for each position and waited for the display to settle before recording a number. The centre bench point was checked twice because a trolley passed behind me during the first reading. The two results are written separately on the sheet, and I have not averaged them. The paint rack points were checked once each. The north mark is closer to the supply grille, and the south mark is beside the lower storage shelf. The grille itself was clear, but a paper tag was tied to its outer edge.

Mara said, “Please leave the tag in place because it belongs to the inventory check, and I will remove it after the count.” I left it there and added the note to the sketch. The tag did not cover the grille opening, but it could be seen from the floor mark. I did not move the storage shelf or any of the tools around it. The workshop lead, Jon, said, “If the loading door is open, the draft reaches the paint rack first.” The loading door remained shut while we were there, and Jon was speaking about the usual afternoon deliveries rather than the morning check.

Then there is the numbered section for the packet:
1. The room sketch has the intake wall, the sink window, the east door, the loading door, and the three reading positions marked in pencil.
2. The reading sheet lists the time, the position, and the displayed value in separate columns, and it keeps the two centre bench entries on separate lines.
3. The equipment note gives the meter and reference unit serial endings and says that the reference unit was within its date.
These are descriptions of what is in the folder, not a summary of what the readings mean. I checked that the pages are in the same order as the index and that the sketch can be read without removing it from the clear sleeve.

There is one condition that matters for the later comparison: if the exterior wind is above twenty-five kilometres per hour when the next check is done, the facilities desk should keep that day's readings separate from these morning readings and note the wind speed on its sheet. That condition is written in the margin of the reading sheet and repeated in the cover note. It is not a request to cancel the next check. The weather board at the workshop entrance showed a lower wind speed at nine o'clock, but I did not copy that figure into the comparison note because the condition concerns the day of the next check.

Before leaving, I asked Mara whether the service calendar had a fixed date. She said the desk was collecting availability and had not set one. She asked me to send the packet by email as well as putting a copy in the internal tray. I told her I could forward the scanned pages after checking that the serial endings were legible. The scan is not attached to this account because I made it after returning to the office. The folder itself remains with me until the facilities desk confirms it has received the paper copy and the email.

At eleven twenty, I checked the scan against the folder and could read all three serial endings without enlarging the image. The tag beside the grille is visible in the room sketch note, and the two centre bench readings remain separate in the scanned sheet. I am forwarding the packet now to the facilities desk with Mara copied on the email, and the paper copy is in the internal tray marked facilities. The calendar date is still unset, and the next comparison will depend on the wind condition written in the margin. I have not added a proposed service date or an interpretation of the readings to the packet.

I am at the north gate of Alder Creek Trail on Tuesday morning with the replacement sign leaning against the inside wall of the tool shed. The old sign is still attached to the post, but the lower right corner has split around two of the screws, and the lettering for the creek crossing is hard to read from the path. The new panel is cedar colored with dark green letters, and it has the same route number seven and the same mileage to the picnic shelter as the old one. I checked those details against the paper map before anyone unloaded the ladder.

Mara from the parks office brought the sign out in a flat cardboard sleeve and set it on two sawhorses so the edges would not drag across the gravel. She said the sleeve should go back in the maintenance truck because the supplier may collect it on the next delivery. The metal brackets are in a separate bag, and one bag has four bolts, washers, and lock nuts, while the small bag has two extra washers. I am forwarding the signed work sheet and the updated map to Leon at the district desk this afternoon. The work sheet has the gate location, the post number, and the name of the crew lead on the first page.

The weather has stayed dry since Monday, but the forecast calls for showers after three, and the north path gets slick when the leaves are wet. We are planning to remove the damaged panel before lunch and keep the post in place because it is straight and does not move when pushed. If the post loosens while the old panel is off, we will stop and call the parks office before mounting anything new. The replacement cannot be installed safely on a leaning post, and there is no spare post in the truck today.

1. Bring the step ladder from the storage bay and put the orange cone on the trail side of the work area.
2. Photograph the old sign in place, including the cracked corner and the post number.
3. Loosen the top screws first while someone supports the lower edge.
4. Put the old panel in the marked return rack rather than leaving it beside the path.
5. Compare the new lettering and route number with the map before tightening the brackets.
6. Record the time the crew leaves the gate in the work sheet. The crew lead asked us not to write a guessed time. If the radio clock and phone clock differ, use the radio clock and note that choice in the margin.

At the trail junction, a family stopped while we were checking the route line, and the father asked whether the picnic shelter was still open. The shelter is open, but the drinking fountain is shut off for seasonal maintenance, and the nearest working fountain is by the lower parking lot. Mara told him the creek bridge has a narrow walking surface and said, “Please keep children beside you while you cross the bridge.” He thanked her and continued toward the shelter. The junction map has a small blue dot for the fountain and a brown square for the shelter, and both marks are still easy to see on the paper copy.

Leon wants the signed work sheet sent with a scan of the old sign photograph because the district file does not include a close view of the damaged corner. The crew lead has already written the post number in the top margin, and Mara has checked the replacement panel against the route map. The map copy for the file is dated April eighth and shows the short connector to the lower parking lot in dotted blue. The public map at the gate is older and does not show that connector, so we should not use it to check the fountain directions. I will label the scan “north gate sign” and include the date on the file name.

Mara said the sign supplier can take the cardboard sleeve only if it is clean and dry, so it will stay in the truck until the delivery driver arrives. If rain starts before the panel is mounted, the crew will cover the replacement with the tarp and postpone the work rather than leave wet cardboard around the brackets. The tarp is folded behind the first aid kit, and the bungee cords are in the side pocket of the ladder bag. The crew lead has the key for the tool shed and will lock it before going back down the service road.

After the site check, we also need to leave the temporary notice at the north gate so hikers know that the crew may be working near the post. The notice says the trail remains open and asks visitors to pass slowly while the ladder is set up. It does not close the creek crossing, and it does not direct people onto the service road. Mara has two clips for the notice, but one clip is bent and should not be used. The other clip fits the wooden rail beside the map case without covering the route number.

When I send the scan and work sheet, Leon can file them with the spring inspection notes, but the replacement date should stay blank until the crew finishes the work. The old panel may be returned to the rack for the parks office to review, and no one has decided whether it will be repaired or recycled. The route map and the photo will make it possible to check the lettering later if a visitor reports that the mileage looks different. The north gate is expected to be busy during the weekend bird walk, so the work area needs to be clear before Friday afternoon. I have packed the small bag of extra washers with the work sheet and will make sure the signed page stays flat during the walk back to the truck.

MODE: /slack
LANGUAGE: en
INPUT:
Mara: Morning from the east ridge. I’ve started the notebook with the date, crew, weather, and map reference: 14 June, dry, light northwest wind, sheet 7B. The ridge is mostly exposed basalt, but loose scree covers the lower approach, so we’re keeping the packs on the marked trail.

Eli: I checked the compass against the phone before we left camp. It’s reading consistently, though the phone’s elevation is about 18 meters higher than the barometric reading. I’ve written down both figures rather than choosing one; the weather station may help us sort that out later.

Mara: Station 14 is at the bend in the trail, beside a patch of dwarf willow. The basalt there has narrow columnar joints, mostly trending northwest, and a thin orange-brown coating on a few faces. The coating rubs off as powder, but we haven’t sampled it yet.

Jon: I’m adding a note about the creek crossing: water is clear, shallow, and moving fast over rounded cobbles. There’s a small bar of pale sand on the inside bend. If the level rises after lunch, we’ll use the higher crossing upstream instead of trying to wade here.

Mara: Good call. I photographed the bar with the scale in frame and noted the camera direction as east. The sand is fine to medium grained, with scattered dark grains; no obvious shell fragments or plant material in the area we checked.

Eli: The first notebook page has the route sketch now. I marked the creek, the old trail stakes, and the two outcrops we can see from the ridge. The northern outcrop looks darker from here, but distance and shadow make that a weak observation until we get closer.

Jon: We’re at the lower exposure. It’s a grey, fine-grained rock with small pale crystals scattered through it. The contacts are covered by soil and grass, so I can’t tell whether this is a separate flow or just a weathered face of the same basalt.

Mara: I wrote “possible flow boundary” with a question mark, not as a confirmed contact. There’s a rusty seam about 4 centimeters wide, dipping gently east. It breaks unevenly and has a few tiny quartz grains, but we don’t have enough evidence yet to call it a vein.

Eli: Numbered notebook section for today’s stops:
1. Creek bend: water, sand bar, and crossing condition.
2. Lower exposure: grey fine-grained rock and uncertain contact.
3. Ridge crest: jointed basalt and weathered surface coating.
I’ll add sample IDs only after the bags and page entries match.

Jon: The lower exposure has three fresh breaks on its north side. They’re less orange than the outer surface, which suggests the color may be from weathering rather than the rock’s original composition. That’s still tentative; we’d need a clean sample and lab work to check it.

Mara: At the crest now. The joints are closer together near the western edge, roughly 15 to 25 centimeters apart, and open only a few millimeters. One joint holds damp moss. The eastern face is drier and has a thin crust that flakes under very light pressure.

Eli: I’ve logged the crest elevation from the map as approximately 1,240 meters, not a GPS fix. The contour interval is 20 meters, and the ridge is broad, so we shouldn’t imply more precision than that. The phone still differs from the barometer by about the same amount.

Jon: Quick weather note: high cloud is moving in from the northwest, but visibility is still good toward the valley. The wind has picked up a little. No rain at the stations so far, though the creek is higher than it was when we crossed this morning.

Mara: That makes the alternate crossing worth keeping in the plan. I checked it from the trail: the upstream section is wider and shallower, with stable gravel on the bank. We’ll only switch if the main crossing becomes unsafe; for now, nobody needs to go back and test it.

Eli: The dark grains in the creek sand are magnetic in a quick hand-magnet check, but that only tells us some grains respond to the magnet. I’ve noted the tool used and kept the observation separate from any mineral identification. Sample bag S-03 is from the dry bar surface.

Jon: I photographed the orange coating at station 14 with a ruler and a card showing the station label. The surface underneath is fractured basalt, not the grey rock from the lower exposure. I’ve put the image number beside the notebook entry so it can be found without guessing.

Mara: Lunch break at the sheltered notch. We compared notes and found one difference in the route sketch: Eli’s creek bend is about 30 meters farther south than mine. We’ll check the map grid before revising either sketch; both entries stay in the book for now.

Eli: Map check done. My mark was misplaced because I used the trail junction as the reference point instead of the creek bend. I’ve corrected the sketch with a single line through the old mark, leaving it readable, and added the grid coordinates from sheet 7B.

Jon: The cloud cover has lowered the light on the north face, so colors are harder to judge than they were this morning. The northern outcrop has visible bands, but from this safe vantage point we can’t tell whether they’re mineral layers, weathering streaks, or shadows along the slope.

Mara: We stopped short of the loose upper slope and recorded the view from firm ground. There are angular blocks below the outcrop, several with pale interiors and dark rinds. The blocks could have fallen from above, but we haven’t traced any of them to a source face.

Eli: I’ve added a notebook reminder to revisit the barometer comparison against station data before we turn these elevations into a profile. If the station’s pressure record is incomplete, we’ll report the map-based elevation only. The two readings are useful field notes, not interchangeable measurements.

Jon: End-of-day inventory: four photo sets, three filled sample bags, and one blank duplicate label returned to the kit. S-03 is the only creek-sand sample; the other two are small basalt chips from separate fresh breaks. All bags have initials and page references.

Mara: Final entry before we head back: the notebook has the route, station observations, photographs, sample references, and uncertainties from today. The creek level is still up, so we’ll take the marked trail to the higher crossing on the return. I’ve recorded that choice beside the morning crossing note and left the original observation unchanged.

Ich habe das Ticket über die App gekauft, von Hamburg Hbf nach Berlin Hbf, für den 18. Mai 2026. Der Zug ist ICE 804 mit Abfahrt um 09:06 Uhr. Auf der Buchungsbestätigung steht „Sparpreis“. INPUT:
Create a reusable page layout for a geology field notebook used during day trips to exposed rock sites. Include spaces for the date, observer, site name or location, weather, route or access notes, and a brief description of the outcrop. Provide separate areas for observations, measurements, sketches, and questions to check later. Make the layout practical to fill in outdoors with a pencil, and keep the labels concise. If a measurement is recorded, include a place to note its units and the method used. If a sketch is made, include a caption area and a way to link it to the relevant observation. Leave unknown details blank rather than suggesting values. The page should support several observations from one site without requiring a separate page for each one. we need an accessibility audit of the Northline library app, specifically the screen-reader experience for finding a branch, reserving a title, and checking the status of an existing hold. The audit should cover the current public release, version 4.8.1, and should be done with the standard text size and default display settings. Please don't treat this as a general visual design review; the question is whether a screen-reader user can understand and complete the same main tasks without guessing.

Please don't change its password, profile details, or notification settings. You can place a reservation on the title River Glass, but don't cancel either of the two existing holds. If the app asks for a pickup branch, choose East Market, and note whether the selected branch is announced after the choice. The title is in the catalog on both platforms, but availability can change during the week, so record what the app shows at the time rather than treating a copy count as fixed.

The audit should include the sign-in path, the search results, the title details screen, the reservation confirmation, and the holds list. For each of those, check whether focus starts in a sensible place, moves in a predictable order, and announces controls with their purpose and state. Please also check whether headings are exposed as headings and whether repeated controls have enough context to distinguish them. In the holds list, there are two buttons labeled “More.” One is for the hold on River Glass and the other is for A Map of Salt. We need to know whether the screen reader announces which hold each button belongs to, not just the word “More.”

For the search task, search for River Glass by title and do not use voice input. Record whether the query can be edited, whether the clear-search control is announced, and whether the result count is spoken when the results load. On the title details screen, check the author, format, availability message, and reservation control. If the reservation control is unavailable because all copies are checked out, do not try to bypass it; record the announced reason and continue with the holds-list checks. If it is available, place the reservation at East Market and check the confirmation message and the updated holds list. In either case, do not remove or edit an existing hold.

Please organize the findings in these sections:
1. Test setup and versions, including the date and time of each session.
2. Task steps and the result on each platform.
3. Screen-reader announcement or focus problems, with the exact screen and control named.
4. Any differences between iOS and Android that affect completing the tasks.
5. Open questions that need a product or library answer.

For an issue, describe the steps needed to encounter it, what VoiceOver or TalkBack announced, and what you expected it to announce. Keep the expected behavior tied to the task, rather than recommending a specific implementation. If a problem happens only after repeating an action, say how many times you repeated it and whether it happened on both platforms. Please don't call a problem intermittent just because it was seen once. If you can't reproduce something, state that plainly and include the path you tried. We also need the app version, operating system, screen reader, and test time next to each finding so that engineering can repeat the same setup.

Mara from the library team said, “The labels are still being reviewed, so please tell us what the reader actually says before suggesting replacement wording.” Please include exact spoken labels when they are relevant, but don't infer a label from the visible text if the screen reader says something different. The team is comparing the audit with a list of known issues, so note whether each finding is new to this session or matches an item already on that list. The list is in the shared Northline folder under Accessibility / Current Issues, and the version there is dated May 6. If you cannot open that folder, leave the match status unconfirmed rather than guessing.

If build 4.8.2 is available in TestFlight by Thursday at noon, repeat the search and reservation checks on that build and label those results separately from the 4.8.1 results; otherwise, complete the requested work on 4.8.1 and state that 4.8.2 was not available by that time. Do not replace the public-release findings with test-build findings. If a serious task-blocking issue is reproducible on 4.8.1, include the steps and platform details in the issue section even if it is fixed in 4.8.2. If it occurs only on 4.8.2, identify that condition and don't describe it as a public-release problem.

Please keep observations separate from confirmed behavior: for example, note if a label sounded clipped, but only say it was clipped if it stopped before the full announcement could be heard. Include any difference caused by the phone's system speech rate only if the default rate was changed during testing; otherwise leave that setting as the default. The library needs the report to compare both platforms and decide what needs follow-up, so make the steps concrete enough that another tester can repeat them, including where focus was immediately before any unexpected announcement. If the reservation could not be placed because availability changed during the session, record the displayed availability and stop at that point rather than describing a confirmation or an updated hold that did not occur.

I usually prefer a compact button in the toolbar, rather than a panel opening by itself when a page loads. The extension currently has a toolbar icon, a side panel, notifications, and a small status mark on supported pages, so I am thinking about how those pieces should relate, not asking to remove all of them.

The first preference I look for is whether the extension is active on a particular site. I would like that choice to be easy to find and easy to reverse, because I sometimes need the feature for a page and sometimes want to read without it. A site switch should apply to the current site, not silently become a setting for every site. I also want a clear difference between pausing the extension temporarily and turning it off for a site. If I pause it, I expect the pause to end when I choose, not because I happen to close the current tab. If I disable it for a site, that site should remain disabled until I change that choice.

Notifications are different: I would like to control them separately from the status mark, since a visible mark can be useful while repeated pop-ups are distracting. I occasionally miss a notification that contains a real change, though, so I would rather not have one universal switch that treats every message in exactly the same way. A setting for important notices and another for routine notices would be easier for me to understand, if the extension has those types of messages.

1. The toolbar button should open the extension controls when I select it; it should not open the side panel automatically.

3. The status mark should remain optional and separate from notifications. If there is no useful status to show on a page, I do not need a blank mark there.
4. The extension should offer a simple way to pause on the current site, with a clear indication of whether it is paused or disabled for that site.

I use the same preferences in different situations, and I do not want a change on one device to surprise me on the other. If I enable sync, I want only the extension preferences to follow my account; saved page content should not be included in that choice. If sync is off, I expect the choices to stay with the browser profile where I made them. This matters because I sometimes use a work computer that has a separate browser profile, and I do not want its extension settings to become mixed with the settings on my home laptop. I might keep sync off most of the time, but I would like the choice to be visible rather than buried in a general account page.

The wording on the preference screen should make the effect of a control clear before I select it. I have seen labels such as “quiet mode” that sound appealing but do not tell me whether they hide the status mark, stop notifications, or both. A short explanation beside a setting would be more useful than a long description in a separate help page. I do not need every preference to have a paragraph under it, and I would rather see a few precise lines than a wall of text. For example, “Pause on this site until I turn it back on” says more to me than a vague label like “temporary.”

I also want the screen to distinguish preferences that affect every site from those that affect only the site I am currently viewing. If I change a general notification preference while looking at a page, that should not make it seem as though I changed the site's individual setting too. The site-specific controls can be grouped together, with the general display and notification controls in another area. I would not put the sync switch next to the pause control, because they have different effects and I could easily mistake one for the other when making a quick change.

There are a few details I am less certain about. I usually keep the side panel narrow, but I might want it wider when I am reviewing a page with a long list of items. Remembering its width would help, provided the panel still stays within the browser window on a smaller screen. I also prefer that the extension remember whether I last opened the panel, but I do not want it to reopen by itself on the next page or after restarting the browser. Those are separate things to me: remembering a size is convenient, while restoring an open panel can feel like an interruption.

When I review the preferences later, I want to be able to tell which choices are global, which are for the current site, and which depend on sync being enabled. The controls can stay compact, but the labels should not make those distinctions hard to notice. I would use a short site name near the site-specific controls and a separate heading for the general preferences. If sync is disabled, its status should still be shown in that area, so I can understand why the settings are staying with this browser profile. The side panel width, the optional status mark, and the two kinds of notification preferences are the details I am most likely to revisit.

payload.instruction:
MODE: /polish
LANGUAGE: en
PROFILE: Clear and professional.
INPUT:
The board-game lending shelf occupies two bookcases beside the community room’s north entrance. Residents may borrow games at no charge, and the shelf is open whenever the building’s front desk is staffed. A laminated sign gives the borrowing steps, the current desk hours, and an email address for questions. The shelf began with a small donation from a neighborhood game club; residents have since contributed most of the collection. Its purpose is practical: make games available to people who want to try them without buying a copy or arranging a private exchange.

Each game has a numbered label on its box and a matching entry in the lending ledger. The entry lists the title, publisher, player range, approximate playing time, and the date the game joined the shelf. A short note identifies features that could affect a borrower’s choice, such as small pieces, a reading requirement, or a play area larger than a kitchen table. The notes describe the contents rather than rate a game. When the group does not know a detail, the entry says so instead of presenting a guess as fact.

Borrowers take a game to the desk and provide their name and a way to contact them. The desk volunteer records the box number, checkout date, and expected return date, then checks that the borrower has received the rules booklet and any loose materials listed on the inventory card. The standard loan is two weeks. A borrower who needs more time may ask for an extension before the due date; if another person has requested that game, the extension may not be available. The volunteer writes down the agreed date so that both parties have the same information.

The return process includes a brief count, not a judgment about whether every item looks new. The borrower and volunteer compare the pieces with the inventory card, place them in their labeled bags, and note any missing or damaged items in the ledger. If a component is missing, the box remains on the desk rather than going back onto the shelf until the volunteer has checked whether the item is in the room or stored with another game. That condition matters because a box that appears complete at a glance can still be missing a small card or token needed during play.

The shelf uses these steps to keep routine lending consistent:

1. Choose a game from the shelves and read its box label and contents note before checkout.
2. Ask the desk volunteer to enter the loan in the ledger and confirm the return date.
3. Keep the rules booklet and the component bags with the game while it is out.
4. Return the box to the desk, where its components can be checked against the inventory card.
5. Tell the volunteer about a missing or damaged piece, even if the rest of the game is present.

The numbered steps are a quick guide, while the inventory card remains the detailed record for each particular box. Some editions of a game contain different pieces, and donated boxes do not always include the same insert or player aid as a newer edition. For that reason, volunteers check the card attached to the individual copy instead of relying on a general list found online. The library does not replace a component merely because it differs from another edition; the relevant question is whether the listed copy’s own contents are accounted for.

Volunteers inspect donations before assigning them a shelf number. They confirm the title and edition where possible, look for the rules, and sort loose pieces into groups that can be counted. If instructions are absent, the donor may be asked whether they have a booklet or a link to the publisher’s rules. A donated game can be set aside while that information is checked, but it is not marked available until the shelf entry and inventory card can describe the copy accurately. A volunteer said, “It is better to leave a space on the shelf than to promise a complete game we have not checked.”

The collection includes cooperative games, word games, abstract strategy games, and longer games designed for groups. The category labels help visitors browse, but they do not guarantee a particular experience: one game may combine several styles, and players’ preferences vary. The box notes provide the most useful details available, including a publisher’s player range when it is printed on the box. For a game with a suggested age range, the shelf records the printed range without treating it as a rule about who is allowed to borrow or play.

Requests for a game that is already on loan are recorded in the ledger with the person’s name and contact information. When the game comes back, the desk volunteer contacts the next person on the list, who has three days to collect it. If that person no longer wants the game, the volunteer moves to the next request. A request does not reserve the game indefinitely, and the return date remains visible in the ledger so that a waiting borrower can understand when the copy is expected back. Staff do not promise a date if a loan is overdue.

The shelf is maintained by volunteers, with the front desk providing a consistent place to check out and return boxes. Volunteers review the ledger each week, follow up on overdue games when contact details are available, and check whether returned boxes have been put back in the correct numbered space. They also note recurring problems, such as a label that has become hard to read or an inventory card that needs clarification. One volunteer described the work simply: “A clear label saves the next person a lot of guessing.”

Residents may send questions about the collection to the email address on the sign, including requests for information about a specific game or a correction to an entry. A question is not treated as a reservation unless the person asks to be added to the waiting list and provides contact details. The shelf’s records are updated when a checked fact changes, such as a revised desk schedule or the discovery of a component stored with the wrong box. The collection therefore depends on both careful records and ordinary communication between borrowers and volunteers.

our college film society meets every wednesday in the media room, which is on the second floor of the library. we watch one film at each meeting, and the person who picks it changes from week to week. after the screening, we talk about what worked and what did not, though the discussion can get a little long if people have different opinions about the ending. membership is open to students from any department, and there is no fee to attend.

for next month, we have booked the small auditorium for a screening of the 1975 film Barry Lyndon on november 14. the doors open at 6:30 p.m., and the film begins at 7. the auditorium has more seats than our usual room, so we are hoping people will bring a friend if they want to. we usually post the film choice and meeting details on the society's noticeboard and group page, but sometimes the post goes up only a few days before the meeting. i think Barry Lyndon is perhaps a slightly unusual choice for us because it is longer than most of the films we have shown this term. still, the screening will be followed by our regular discussion, and students can leave whenever they need to.
payload.response:

After the screening, we talk about what worked and what didn’t. The discussion can run a little long when people have different opinions about the ending. Membership is open to students from any department, and there is no fee to attend.

Next month, we have booked the small auditorium for a screening of the 1975 film Barry Lyndon on November 14. The doors open at 6:30 p.m., and the film begins at 7. The auditorium has more seats than our usual room, so we hope people will bring a friend if they wish. We usually post the film choice and meeting details on the society’s noticeboard and group page, though sometimes the post goes up only a few days before the meeting. I think Barry Lyndon may be a slightly unusual choice for us because it is longer than most of the films we have shown this term. The screening will be followed by our regular discussion, and students can leave whenever they need to.

Wir sind zwei Erwachsene und zwei Kinder im Alter von acht und elf Jahren. Von Montag bis Mittwoch sollte die Zubereitung höchstens 30 Minuten dauern. Für Donnerstag ist ein Resteessen vorgesehen; plane dafür Reste von den vorherigen Abendessen ein. Am Freitag darf die Zubereitung länger dauern. Mindestens ein Abendessen soll vegetarisch sein. Ein Kind mag keine Pilze, Allergien gibt es keine.

Das Budget für die fünf Abendessen beträgt ungefähr 75 Euro. Reis, Nudeln, Öl und Salz sind bereits vorhanden und sollen nicht auf der Einkaufsliste stehen.

Gib für jeden Abend ein konkretes Essen und die wichtigsten Zutaten an. Achte dabei auf die genannten Zeit- und Budgetvorgaben. Ergänze danach eine Einkaufsliste mit den benötigten Mengen, soweit diese angegeben werden können.

**Ausgabeformat:**
- Stelle den Essenskalender als Tabelle mit einem Eintrag für jeden Wochentag dar.
- Schreibe die Einkaufsliste anschließend als nummerierte Checkliste, die beim Einkaufen abgehakt werden kann, nicht als Tabelle.
- Nimm nichts für Frühstück oder Mittagessen auf.

def batch_records(records, width=56):
