Maya: One question on the saddle. If the rubber seat is torn or has a cut across the sealing face, replace the saddle and use the spare clamp; if the seat is intact, keep the saddle and replace only the tee and its clamps. Please take a photo before removing it either way.

Ben: That works. I’ll label the photos “west tee,” “upstream side,” and include the ruler in the frame. The last set of pictures didn’t show the clamp position, so this time I’ll get one wide shot of the box and one close shot before anything moves.

Ana: The orchard map in the truck still shows the old row numbers near the drainage ditch. I’ve taped a corrected copy beside the radio charger; pear 48 is row 12, and the next hydrant west is marked H-6. Use that map if the crew asks for access.

Luis: The irrigation schedule says the west block runs 7:15 to 9:00, but that’s the usual slot, not a promise that the repair will be done by 9. I can move the next west set to 12:30 if we get the valve back and the pressure check is clean.

Maya: Yes, hold the 12:30 slot as the backup. Don’t start that set just because the tee is closed up. We need the box clear, the clamps checked, and a steady reading at the west gauge for five minutes before we put the block back on schedule.

Ben: I’ll bring the hand tamper too. Once the leak is fixed, we can backfill in layers, but let’s leave the top six inches loose until we’ve run the short test. The box lid rocks if the soil settles under its northwest corner, so we should tamp that side carefully.

Ana: I’ll ask the picking crew to leave the first two bins off the north lane until 11. They’re loading pears from rows 10 and 11 that morning, and the forklift needs the wider turn by the shed. If repair work runs late, they can use the south lane instead.

Luis: The spare clamp is stainless and fits the repair coupling, but it’s not the same width as the older clamp on the saddle. I’ve put both sizes in separate bags and marked them with tape. Don’t use the narrow one on the coupling; it won’t cover the full band.

Maya: Just to keep the sequence clear:
1. Close the west block valve and confirm the east block is still running.
2. Open the box, photograph the saddle, then inspect the rubber seat before choosing the repair branch.
3. After assembly, run the short test with the box open and check the gauge before backfilling.

Ben: I’ll read the gauge at the inlet and west side before the valve closes, then again after the test. If the west header is still below 18 psi after we close the north valve, isolate the upper block and keep the lower block running; otherwise, leave both blocks on the current schedule and recheck at 2. The north valve is the one beside H-6, not the gate valve by the shed.

Ana: Thanks for spelling that out. I’ll put a tag on H-6 so nobody grabs the wrong handle. The upper block feeds rows 12 through 16, and the lower block feeds rows 8 through 11, so I’ll let the picking lead know which rows might be affected if we have to isolate the upper side.

Luis: If the pressure stays under 18 after that isolation, don’t keep cycling the pump to chase it. Message me the two readings and whether the west gauge needle is steady or bouncing. I can check the filter and the pump log from the shed, but I won’t change the setpoint remotely.

Maya: Right, and please include the time with each reading. We had two notes last month that just said “pressure low,” and nobody could tell whether they were taken before or after the valve change. A photo of both gauges is fine if the numbers are readable.

Ben: I’ll also bring the lockout tag for the west valve and a second flashlight. The box is shaded by the pear canopy by 8, and the headlamp battery in the repair kit didn’t hold a charge last time. The crew can use the portable work light from the pump shed if needed.

Ana: I checked with picking, and they can keep the bins clear until 11. They’ll need the north lane again after that to move the full bins, so please tell me by 10:30 if the trailer or mini excavator is still blocking the turn. I can redirect them, but not without a little notice.

Maya: Final check for Thursday: bring the listed fittings, both clamp sizes, the gauge kit, and the spare hose washer; keep the east block on its normal cycle; and use the seat condition to choose which repair branch to follow. If we need the upper-block isolation, post the readings and time here before changing the picking plan. The 12:30 west set stays on hold until the test is steady for five minutes and the box is clear.

LANGUAGE: en
PROFILE: Friendly and conversational.
INPUT:

our board-game lending shelf is in the east room of the Marlow Community Hall, between the noticeboard and the low radiator. It began in April 2022, when three members of the Wednesday supper group brought in games they had stopped playing at home. The hall committee agreed that the shelf could stay there, and the group now looks after it. There are two wide shelves, a small basket for cards and dice, and a clipboard on a hook at the side. The window above the shelf gets afternoon light, though the room is usually dim when the evening meetings begin. We put a paper label on each box with its shelf number, and a matching number is written in the lending book.

The collection has grown to 46 games, not all of which are suitable for the same occasion. There are short games that take about fifteen minutes, longer strategy games, family games, and a few games that are more enjoyable with a larger group. The red sticker means a game is generally playable in under half an hour, while the blue sticker means that it is usually best with at least four people. These are guides rather than rules, since some groups play quickly and others take their time. We have three copies of Orchard Road because it was requested often last winter, and one copy of Lantern Market, which is newer and has only been borrowed twice so far. A couple of boxes are slightly worn around the corners, but their contents have been checked.

People can borrow a game for up to two weeks. They write their name, the game number, and the date taken out in the book, then add the return date when they bring it back. The usual arrangement is to return games on Wednesday evening, when one of the supper group members is at the hall, but borrowers can also leave them with the caretaker during opening hours. If a game is returned with a piece missing, it is placed in the basket marked “Needs checking” rather than put straight back on the shelf. That detail matters because the caretaker does not check game contents, and another borrower might otherwise take the box before anyone notices. We check the piece list in the box and note any missing item in the book before deciding whether the game can go back out.

There is a short note inside the lending book that says, “Please let us know if a box is damaged or a piece is missing.” It is there so people are not worried about bringing something back in imperfect condition. In February, a borrower returned Fox and Fable with a split cardboard insert, but all the cards and counters were present. The group taped the insert on the inside, and the game was available again the following week. We do not charge people for ordinary wear, and nobody has been asked to replace a game. Occasionally, a box comes back later than the date written down; we send a friendly reminder rather than treating it as a problem. Most people return games on time, and a few borrowers write the date in their phone as soon as they sign the book.

1. When a new game is donated, we first check that the box has a title and that the contents list is included. One person counts the pieces, while another reads the list, which takes a little longer but makes mix-ups less likely. The game then gets a number in the order it is added, a label, and a line in the book with its title and player range. If the instructions are in another language, we note that on the label so borrowers can see it before taking the game. The group does not make a new set of rules for a game, and donations are not added until the contents have been checked.

2. On Wednesday evenings, the person on shelf duty looks over the book and checks whether any game is due back. They also put returned boxes on the table for a quick look before replacing them. If the weather has been wet, we leave a box on the table until the outside is dry, because damp cardboard can soften at the edges. The shelf duty is shared among six members, and a simple rota is clipped to the inside of the cupboard door. If the person named on the rota cannot come, they usually arrange a swap in the group chat; the rota is updated only when the swap is confirmed.

3. The lending shelf is for people who use the hall, but a borrower does not need to be a member of the supper group. A small card beside the clipboard gives the borrowing steps and explains that games should not be left outside the hall entrance. The hall closes at nine, so anyone using the caretaker handover needs to return the box before that time. We have not put a deposit system in place. Perhaps that would suit a much larger collection, but at the moment the book and the Wednesday check have been enough to keep track of what is out.

The group talks about the shelf at its monthly supper, usually for only a few minutes because there are other things to arrange. In March, one person suggested setting aside a shelf for games that work well with two players, and the group agreed to try it with the next three donations. The space is not marked yet, and no games have been moved; the idea is to see whether borrowers use that category before changing the labels. Another member said, “I like knowing there’s something new to try, even when I only have an hour.” That comment came up while people were discussing the shorter games, rather than the collection as a whole. The current signs are handwritten on cream card, and one is slightly crooked because the tape keeps lifting near the radiator.

A folding table is sometimes set beside the shelf during the hall’s autumn open evening, so visitors can look through games without blocking the noticeboard. The group has not decided whether to do that this year, because the open evening date has not been confirmed. If it goes ahead, the shelf team would bring out only the games that have complete pieces and keep the lending book by the clipboard, not on the table. This is the same check used on ordinary Wednesday returns. The room is shared with a sewing circle on Thursday afternoons, and their members leave the games where they are; the shelf is not part of their equipment. The caretaker asked for a second basket last month, and the group has placed one beneath the clipboard for the cards and dice that occasionally turn up loose after a game night.

The little collection is still managed by the Wednesday group, with donations coming in at different times rather than through a formal drive. The member who records new games writes in pencil first, in case a title needs correcting, and inks the entry after the label has been checked. We usually hear about a possible donation before it arrives, though once a box was left with the caretaker without a note, and the group waited until the donor was identified before adding it. On the shelf, the games are arranged by number, not by type, because that makes the lending book quicker to use. A printed list of the titles is kept on the table near the door for people who want to browse before walking across the room. The radiator is turned down during the warmer months, but the shelf stays in the same place year-round.

we're preparing the subtitle file for the Meridian Room concert on October 12, and the current file is named `meridian_1012_en_v6.srt`. please clean up the wording and timing notes before we send it to the venue, but keep the original timecodes unless a timing change is specifically listed below. the file covers the full 78-minute set, including the spoken introduction and the encore. It is not supposed to include the audience questions after the encore, because those were not recorded on the camera feed. The audio mix supplied by Jo Alvarez is the source for spoken words; the printed set list is only a reference for song titles and order.

The venue's production manager, Lila Chen, said, “We can send the final set list before lunch, but the lighting team's copy may still show the old order.” If Lila sends the revised set list by 3 p.m. on Friday, update the song-title cards to match it and use the revised order throughout the file. If she does not send it by then, leave the titles in the approved order already shown in v6 and mark the three uncertain spellings in the handoff notes; do not guess from the lighting team's copy. The uncertain spellings are “Morrowglass,” “Aster Vale,” and “Northbound Again.” The first and third are the titles of songs, while Aster Vale is the guest vocalist's name, not a song title. Keep that distinction even if the revised list puts the name beside a song entry.

The first 90 seconds contain the stage manager's introduction, with two speaker changes and a short audience response. The stage manager is identified as Mara Bell in the venue notes, and the response is not assigned to a named speaker. Please use “MARA BELL” for the introduction label, then use “AUDIENCE” for the response only where the response is audible. Do not label general cheering as speech. At 01:14, Mara says, “The doors are behind you, not at the stage.” Keep the word “not”; the venue safety coordinator asked that the direction remain exact. The following sentence in the draft says the exits are on the left, but the audio says “on your right,” so correct that line to match the audio rather than the draft.

1. Please keep each subtitle block to two lines or fewer and aim for no more than 42 characters per line, counting spaces. If a spoken line exceeds 42 characters, split it at a natural pause when one is audible. If there is no natural pause, use two consecutive subtitle blocks with the same speaker label rather than squeezing the whole line into one block. Do not split a person's name across lines. For the phrase “we were waiting at the river gate,” the breath falls after “waiting,” so keep that break in the subtitles. The phrase is spoken twice, once in the introduction and once during the last song, and the two occurrences should retain their separate timecodes.

2. The file has a few lines where the performer sings over a spoken announcement. Keep both voices only when both are intelligible. Where the words cannot be understood, leave the existing “[inaudible]” text in place; do not replace it with a guess based on the lyrics sheet. At 34:08, the announcement is clear but the sung words are not, so retain the announcement and “[inaudible]” as separate subtitle blocks. At 51:22, both voices are clear, and the current blocks already have separate timecodes. Please do not combine those blocks just to make the page look shorter.

3. The draft uses curly apostrophes in contractions, straight apostrophes in possessives, and inconsistent capitalization for repeated speaker labels. Standardize apostrophes to curly marks and make the speaker labels consistent, while leaving song titles in their supplied capitalization. The recurring label for the keyboard player should be “ELI PARK,” not “ELI.” The venue notes list the player's full name, and at the sound check he is introduced by that name. Keep “MARA BELL,” “ELI PARK,” and “AUDIENCE” in capitals wherever they are used as labels; do not change a person's spoken words to capitals.

The subtitle export is intended for the venue's 16:9 screen, not for the band's square social clips. The venue asked for a blank line between subtitle blocks, UTF-8 encoding, and no speaker-color markup because its playback system assigns colors automatically. The current file includes a note at the top saying “Draft for social cut.” Remove that note from the subtitle file, but retain it in the internal handoff notes so the production team can see why the earlier layout differed. Please don't resize or crop the video; this request is only about the subtitle file and the notes sent with it.

There is also a quiet passage after the second song where the guitarist, Eli Park, says, “I thought we left the red case by the stairs.” The venue coordinator asked whether “red case” might instead be “rent case,” but the mix is clear enough to hear “red case.” Keep the audio-supported wording and do not add the coordinator's question to the subtitles. In the next block, the singer says, “It’s still there, I checked.” Preserve the contraction and the comma rather than rewriting it as two sentences. The line appears at 22:41, and the timecode should stay as supplied unless the audio review shows that the block starts more than half a second late.

Before exporting, please check the following items in order:
1. Confirm that the opening introduction and encore are present, and that no audience questions have been added after the encore.
2. Apply the set-list branch described above, using Friday at 3 p.m. as the cutoff, and record the three uncertain spellings in the handoff notes only if the revised list is not received by then.
3. Check the 42-character line target, speaker labels, apostrophes, and the separate overlapping-voice blocks against the audio.
4. Export the subtitle file with the venue's blank-line and UTF-8 requirements, without speaker-color markup, and keep the square-social note out of the file itself.

If the audio review shows that the 22:41 block starts more than half a second late, adjust only that block's start time to the audible beginning of the sentence and leave its end time unchanged. If it does not start more than half a second late, keep both supplied timecodes unchanged. The venue has not asked for a revised video or a lyric transcript, so those should not be included with this delivery. The handoff notes should identify whether the revised set list arrived by the deadline, list any spellings that remain uncertain under the fallback branch, and state that the spoken announcement at 34:08 was retained while the sung words remained inaudible. Please keep those notes factual and limited to the checks described here.

MODE: /transcribe
LANGUAGE: en
INPUT:
The family photo importer is a small program that copies photographs from phones, memory cards, and shared folders into a household archive. Its job is deliberately narrower than a general photo-management application: it identifies files, preserves the originals, records useful metadata, and places each accepted file in a predictable folder. It does not edit images or decide which pictures are worth keeping. That distinction makes maintenance easier, because a change to the importer should not quietly alter the family’s photographs or their history.

The importer runs on a desktop computer when someone connects a device or selects a folder. Before copying anything, it lists the source files and checks their extensions, sizes, and available date information. The supported formats include JPEG, PNG, HEIC, and a small set of camera RAW formats used by relatives who still bring a dedicated camera on trips. Unsupported files are reported in the review log rather than deleted or renamed. A video file may be recorded as skipped, but it is not treated as a failed photograph. The log identifies the source folder and file name so that a family member can find the item again.

The archive is arranged first by year and then by event or source. A folder might be named “2024-07 Lake weekend,” while an image inside keeps its original camera filename. The importer can suggest a date-based folder from metadata, but the person running it chooses or confirms the destination. This matters when a camera clock was wrong, or when a group of scanned prints has no trustworthy capture date. For scans, the family may use the year the prints were made, the year they were scanned, or a known event date; the importer stores the chosen date as archive information without pretending that it came from the camera.

1. Review and copy sequence

First, the program builds a manifest containing the source path, file size, available timestamps, detected format, and a checksum. It compares that information with the archive index and shows possible matches before copying. A matching checksum is strong evidence that two files have identical contents, but a matching name alone is not enough to call them duplicates. Relatives often have files named IMG_0001.JPG, and two unrelated cameras can produce the same name. If the checksum matches, the importer can offer to leave the existing archive copy in place while recording the new source location in the log.

Next, the person reviews proposed folders and any warnings. A file with missing date metadata can still be imported if the destination is chosen manually. If the source becomes unavailable during copying, the importer stops that file, reports the problem, and leaves the rest of the review available. It does not mark a partial copy as complete. Once a file has been copied, the program verifies its checksum against the manifest and records the result. If verification fails, it keeps the source untouched and flags the archive copy for inspection instead of quietly replacing either version.

archive.retain_originals

MODE: /polish
LANGUAGE: de
PROFILE: Friendly and conversational.
INPUT:
Die Reparatur der Gegensprechanlage im Mehrfamilienhaus an der Lindenstraße 18 begann am Dienstag, dem 14. Mai, um neun Uhr. Betroffen waren die Klingel- und Sprechanlage am Haupteingang sowie die Türöffnerfunktion für die Wohnungen im ersten bis dritten Stock. Das Haus hat zwölf Wohnungen und einen kleinen Laden im Erdgeschoss. Die Hausverwaltung hatte die Arbeiten eine Woche zuvor angekündigt; deshalb war der Zugang zum Eingangsbereich frei, und die Bewohner wussten, dass es während des Vormittags zeitweise nicht klingeln würde.

Der beauftragte Techniker, Herr Yilmaz, traf mit einer Werkzeugtasche, einem Spannungsprüfer und einem Ersatznetzteil ein. Hausmeisterin Frau Krüger öffnete ihm den Technikschrank im Flur und zeigte ihm den alten Schaltplan, der in einer Klarsichthülle an der Innenseite der Tür befestigt war. Auf dem Plan waren einige frühere Änderungen mit Kugelschreiber eingetragen. Frau Krüger sagte: „Die Taste für Wohnung 2B funktioniert meistens, aber dort hört man Besucher nur sehr leise.“ Sie erklärte außerdem, dass der Summer im Laden seit dem vergangenen Winter gelegentlich weiterklingele, obwohl die Haustür schon geschlossen sei.

Zuerst prüfte Herr Yilmaz die Spannungsversorgung und die Sicherungen im Schrank. Das vorhandene Netzteil lieferte ungleichmäßige Werte, und an zwei Klemmen waren die Schrauben locker. Er fotografierte die Verdrahtung, bevor er etwas löste, und verglich die Anschlüsse mit dem Schaltplan. Dabei stellte sich heraus, dass ein zusätzliches Kabel für den Laden nach einer früheren Änderung anders geführt worden war als auf der Zeichnung. Die Leitung war nicht beschädigt, doch die abweichende Führung erklärte, weshalb der Summer dort manchmal noch ein kurzes Signal abgab.

Für die Prüfung der einzelnen Sprechstellen bat der Techniker Frau Krüger, nacheinander die Klingeltasten zu drücken und von jeder Wohnung aus zu antworten. Sie ging mit ihm die Liste der Namen am Haustableau durch: Beck, Demir, Hoffmann, Ionescu, Keller, Nguyen, Özdemir, Peters, Rossi, Schneider, Vogel und Weber. Die Bewohnerin aus 2B war zu Hause und nahm an der Prüfung teil. Sie sagte: „Jetzt höre ich Sie klarer, aber bitte testen Sie auch den Türöffner; der hat letzte Woche zweimal nicht reagiert.“ Herr Yilmaz notierte den Hinweis, ohne die Ursache schon festzulegen.

1. Vor dem Austausch des Netzteils wurde die Anlage spannungsfrei geschaltet und gegen unbeabsichtigtes Einschalten gesichert.
2. Die gelösten Klemmen wurden nach der fotografierten Anschlussfolge befestigt; die Leitung zum Laden blieb dabei zunächst unangetastet.
3. Das alte Netzteil wurde durch ein passendes Ersatzgerät mit derselben vorgesehenen Ausgangsspannung ersetzt.
4. Anschließend prüfte Herr Yilmaz die Spannung an der Haustafel und an den Leitungen zu den Wohnungen.
5. Erst nach diesen Messungen nahm er die Sprechanlage wieder in Betrieb und testete Klingel, Sprechverbindung und Türöffner einzeln.

Beim ersten Test nach dem Austausch klingelten die Wohnungen zuverlässig, und die Stimmen waren an beiden Enden verständlich. Der Türöffner reagierte zunächst nur, wenn die Taste länger gedrückt wurde. Herr Yilmaz prüfte deshalb den Kontakt an der Haustafel und maß die Spannung während des Öffnungsvorgangs. Der Kontakt war verschmutzt, aber nicht gebrochen. Nachdem er ihn gereinigt und wieder eingesetzt hatte, ließ sich die Tür mit einem kurzen Tastendruck öffnen. Frau Krüger wiederholte den Test von der Hausmeisterwohnung aus; auch dort funktionierte der Taster ohne Verzögerung.

Danach wandte sich der Techniker dem Summer im Laden zu. Er folgte der Leitung anhand des Fotos und der handschriftlichen Einträge, statt sich nur auf den alten Plan zu verlassen. An einer Verbindung im Schrank saß ein Draht nicht fest genug. Herr Yilmaz befestigte ihn und prüfte die Anlage erneut mit geschlossener Haustür. Falls der Summer danach weiterhin nachklingelt, sollte die Verwaltung einen gesonderten Termin vereinbaren, weil dann auch die Taste am Ladeneingang und der dortige Taster untersucht werden müssten. Für den erneuten Test blieb Frau Krüger im Flur, während Herr Yilmaz draußen an der Haustür die Klingel betätigte.

Bei der abschließenden Runde wurden alle zwölf Klingeltasten der Reihe nach geprüft. Die Bewohner antworteten entweder selbst oder hatten ihre Sprechstellen vorher mit Frau Krüger getestet. Auch die Bewohnerin aus 2B bestätigte, dass die Lautstärke nun ausreiche und der Türöffner sofort reagiere. Für den Laden wurde zweimal geklingelt; nach dem Schließen der Haustür verstummte der Summer jeweils direkt. Herr Yilmaz erklärte, dass er die Anschlussfolge und die Messwerte auf dem Arbeitszettel festhalten werde, damit spätere Arbeiten nicht allein auf dem älteren Plan beruhen.

Frau Krüger legte den Arbeitszettel in die Mappe der Hausverwaltung und notierte daneben das Datum, den Namen des Technikers sowie die Bezeichnung des eingesetzten Netzteils. Den alten Schaltplan ließ sie in seiner Hülle, ergänzte aber einen Vermerk mit dem Hinweis auf die veränderte Leitung zum Laden. Im Flur blieb ein kurzes Informationsblatt hängen, auf dem die Bewohner gebeten wurden, Störungen künftig mit Wohnung, Uhrzeit und Art des Problems zu melden. So konnten spätere Hinweise zu Klingel, Sprechverbindung oder Türöffner genauer zugeordnet und mit den festgehaltenen Messwerten verglichen werden.

Okay, I'm checking the family photo importer before we run it on Mom's old laptop, and I want to keep the folder names exactly as they are. The test card has 286 photos and 19 folders, so please have the preview show both counts separately, not as one total. The first test is just the folder called “2008 summer,” and it should import into the family archive without changing the dates. Can you have the importer prefer the camera date when it exists and leave the scan date alone when it doesn't? Could you keep the last successful import date visible too? That's one date for the whole import, not a date beside every photo. And please don't rename anything automatically, even if two files have the same name.

payload.response:
We opened the repair cafe in the old library meeting room on the second Saturday of April because the community hall roof was being checked and we could not use the usual tables. The room has a side entrance, a low sink, and a narrow cupboard where the library kept folding chairs. Our sign was taped to the glass, and the first visitors came in before we had finished setting up. Nobody seemed bothered by the boxes in the aisle, but we moved them before anyone brought in a heavy appliance.

The welcome table is going to be beside the sink so visitors can wash their hands before they handle a donated object and keep the entrance clear. We borrowed two green cloths from the library and used one to cover the table. The other cloth stayed folded near the kettle because we were not sure whether the sink would be needed for rinsing parts. Mara took names and wrote down what each person hoped to repair. She asked visitors to describe the problem rather than promising that every item could be fixed. A man brought a radio that hummed but gave no sound, and a child arrived with a wooden toy whose wheel had come loose.

We agreed on the room plan while the kettle warmed. The extension lead ran along the wall and was covered with a rubber cable ramp. The volunteer who watched the doorway asked people not to step over the lead, even though it looked flat. We put the first aid kit on the cupboard shelf and the fire exit map beside the light switch. The back window would stay unlocked during the session, but we kept the door itself closed because the latch had caught the previous week. The room was busy and warm, so we opened the upper window for air and checked that nobody had left a bag beneath it. One of the library staff said, “Please leave the chairs in a clear line along the far wall because a reading group needs them on Monday.” We did that and left a gap beside the cupboard for the folding trolley.

Our volunteers had different levels of experience, and we made that clear on the sign at the entrance. The electrical bench was for items that could be unplugged before inspection, and anything with a damaged power cord went into a red tray until a qualified volunteer could look at it. Nobody was asked to open a sealed battery pack. Jo checked small kitchen appliances while Priya handled lamps and desk fans. There were safety glasses for visitors who wanted to watch, but children had to stay with an adult and away from the soldering station. Priya will lead the soldering bench because Jon has to leave before lunch to collect his mother. The soldering station stayed on the far table with a heatproof mat and a metal stand for the iron. Jon still helped sort screws into jars and showed two new volunteers how to test a switch without touching bare wire. We kept spare fuses in labeled drawers rather than putting loose ones on the table.

The first repair was a desk lamp with a cracked plug casing. The owner said it had been flickering for weeks and then stopped after she moved it to another room. Priya saw that the cord insulation was split near the plug and did not connect it to the test socket. She explained that the cafe could replace the plug if the cord itself was still sound, but this cord had to be replaced too. The owner agreed to leave the lamp for a closer inspection and wrote her phone number on the repair card. The radio made a low hum when Jo checked it, and its speaker wire had slipped from a small connector. He reattached the wire and tested the radio at low volume before giving it back. The visitor stayed beside him and said, “My father used to listen to the weather on this every morning, so I am glad it is making a sound again.” The wooden toy took longer because the loose wheel had worn its wooden peg thin. We did not glue it immediately. We showed the child and her grandmother the worn part and asked whether they wanted us to fit a new peg. The grandmother said yes and kept the old wheel in a paper envelope.

At midday we stopped repairs for a short safety check and counted the items waiting on the shelf. The count was seven, not six, and we wrote that number on the board so the afternoon volunteers could compare it with the cards. We made a list for the next session:
1. Ask the library whether we can borrow their small vice again.
2. Bring another rubber cable ramp because the spare one has a split edge.
3. Call the lamp owner after testing the replacement cord.
4. Keep the radio repair card until Jo has added the name of the connector he used.
5. Check with the caretaker about the window latch before the next cafe.

The list was read aloud, and one volunteer pointed out that the vice belonged to the tool club, not the library, so we wrote “tool club” on the note rather than sending the question to the wrong person. The split ramp was placed in a box marked “Do not use,” and nobody took it back to the floor.

After lunch two visitors came in with a hand mixer that smelled hot and a small fan that rattled when it turned. We unplugged the mixer and left it on the inspection tray because the owner could not remember whether it had been used after the smell started. The fan had a loose grille screw and a buildup of dust around the guard. The volunteer removed the grille with the owner watching and cleaned the dust with a soft brush. The blades turned freely afterward, but we asked the owner to try it at home while standing nearby and to bring it back if the rattle returned. We did not use compressed air because it could have pushed dust into the motor. A teenager helped sort the donated screws by length and found three that fit the fan grille. We kept the other screws in separate jars rather than guessing where they belonged.

We had planned to pack away at three, but the caretaker said the room was booked until half past three for a language class, so we kept the tool tables in place and moved the finished items to the windowsill. Each owner checked their own card before leaving, and the radio owner signed that he had collected it. The lamp remained in the cupboard because the replacement cord had not arrived. The hand mixer stayed in the red tray, and its owner took a card with the cafe contact details. If the cupboard still smells damp on Friday, we will leave its door open and ask the library staff to check the pipe behind it before putting tools away there again. The caretaker showed us a small water mark low on the wall but did not know when it had appeared, so we wrote the date beside it and told the library contact what we had seen.

Before we locked up, we counted the chairs and returned the trolley to the side entrance. The first aid kit was still on the shelf, and the exit map had not been covered by the sign. We wiped the table near the sink and left the second green cloth folded where the library staff could find it. Mara put the repair cards in an envelope for the next session, and the volunteers took home only their own labeled tools. We wrote down that the cafe had repaired the radio and toy while the lamp and mixer still needed follow-up. The room was quieter by then, and the caretaker asked us to use the side entrance when we came back the following month. We thanked her and made a note to bring fresh tape for the glass sign because one corner had started to peel during the afternoon. The last visitor had already gone when we turned off the lights and checked that the upper window was shut.

i'm trying to get the winter screening plan for the Bellwether College Film Society into one readable note, because the details are spread across the room request, volunteer chat, and the first draft of our calendar. The series is called “Cold Frames” and it is meant to give people a warm place to land on four Wednesday evenings in January and February. The dates we're working with are January 14, January 21, January 28, and February 4. None of the film titles or dates should be treated as a new announcement; this is still a planning note for the society committee, and I want the open questions to stay open.

The four films on the draft list are The Glass Orchard, Northbound, Paper Moons, and Last Ferry, in that order. We chose them because the first two are quiet and wintery, the third has a funny middle section, and the last one should make for a good discussion about endings. That's the reason for the sequence, not a claim that every member has already seen or approved the films. I would like the note to say that the committee is still checking that the titles can be screened, and that we haven't received a final confirmation about any rights yet.

Humanities 204 is the room we have asked to use for all four evenings. Its listed capacity is 68 seats, which makes it easier for us to keep the group together and leave the front rows open for people who need to leave early. The booking is not confirmed. The room coordinator said, “I can probably hold those dates, but I need to check the lecture timetable first.” Please keep that as a tentative statement rather than making it sound like the room is ours.

If Humanities 204 is not confirmed by December 3, we should ask about Studio B instead. Studio B has a listed capacity of 42 seats, so if that is the room we get, we would need to change the sign-up limit to 42 and tell members that seating is more limited. Don't make the Studio B request sound automatic; it only becomes our next step if we don't have confirmation for Humanities 204 by December 3. If neither room is available, I don't yet know what we should do, and the note shouldn't choose another venue for us.

For each evening, we need two volunteers at the entrance, one person to check the caption file, and one person to lead the discussion after the film. At the moment, six people have said they might be available for at least one evening, but nobody has committed to all four. We should ask people to mark which dates they can do, rather than assign names to jobs now. A member said, “I can help with the door, but I can't promise every Wednesday,” and that's a useful example of why we need date-by-date replies.

The caption files need a check before each screening, even though the distributor's listing says captions are included. We should not assume that the caption file will work on our player just because it is listed. One volunteer can test the file on the society laptop, then tell the projection lead whether the captions appear in sync. I don't know yet who will take that task. If a file does not work, we need to flag it to the committee before that evening, but we have not decided what replacement option is available.

We have a small winter hospitality budget of $180 for the whole series, not $180 per screening. I was thinking we could use it for tea, paper cups, and a simple snack table, but I don't have prices yet, so please leave the spending plan as a suggestion rather than a settled purchase. The society has already asked the student union whether we may use the kitchenette, and we are waiting for an answer. If the kitchenette is unavailable, we'd need to rethink how we serve tea; I haven't worked out an alternative and don't want one invented in this note.

There are also a few practical details from the last screening that should be included without turning them into firm rules for every event. People arrived in a rush just before the film started, so a 15-minute door period would give volunteers time to check names and direct people to seats. We printed 40 programme cards last time and ran short, but we don't know how many people will come to this series. For now, we can ask whether it makes sense to print more than 40, without naming a new print quantity. The committee also mentioned that the entrance gets drafty, which is why the winter supplies list may be useful.

1. Before each date, confirm the room, volunteer replies, and caption-file check. The room confirmation matters first because the 68-seat limit belongs to Humanities 204, while Studio B has 42 seats. If the room changes, we need to adjust the sign-up information before members rely on it. Please keep the room condition and the different capacities together in the note so nobody reads the larger limit as applying to both spaces.
2. Ask the committee to review the $180 total hospitality budget and decide whether tea, paper cups, and snacks are workable after we get prices and hear about the kitchenette. The Saturday shift at the Harbor Street charity kitchen began before sunrise, while rain tapped against the loading-bay door and the street outside was still quiet. Mara, the shift coordinator, unlocked the pantry at 5:45 and checked the whiteboard before anyone started cooking. The plan was to serve lunch to about 140 people, but the number was only an estimate because the nearby shelter had reported several new arrivals overnight. Mara said, “Let’s prepare enough for the estimate, and keep the extra rice dry until we know how many guests are coming.” That decision mattered later, when the shelter called with an updated count.

Six volunteers arrived between six and six-thirty. Two had worked the kitchen before; the others were first-time helpers from a local college. Mara paired each new volunteer with someone who knew the room, then showed everyone where the hand-washing sink, gloves, fire blanket, and first-aid kit were kept. The kitchen’s printed temperature chart was clipped beside the refrigerator, and Leon checked the cooler before moving in the donated vegetables. It read 38 degrees Fahrenheit, within the kitchen’s safe range. A box of tomatoes had split during delivery, so the volunteers set aside the damaged fruit for immediate use rather than placing it in storage. The remaining produce was counted and recorded on the donation sheet.

The menu included lentil stew, rice, roasted carrots, bread, and apples. A donor had brought carrots from a neighborhood garden, along with a note saying they had been harvested the previous afternoon. Priya rinsed and peeled them while Ben cut them into even pieces. Mara asked the team to keep the vegetable scraps in the marked compost bin, not the regular trash. The lentils had already been sorted the night before, but the cooking group still rinsed them in batches and checked for small stones. When the large stockpot reached a steady simmer, Leon lowered the heat so the bottom would not scorch. He tasted a spoonful and said, “It needs a little more salt, but let’s wait until the broth has reduced.” Nobody added seasoning until the next tasting.

1. At 7:10, Mara divided the remaining preparation work. The first table washed and portioned apples, the second arranged bread in paper bags, and the third prepared labels for meals that needed to be carried to the shelter. Each label listed the meal’s date and the main ingredients. The kitchen did not claim that any meal was free of every possible allergen, so Mara told the volunteers to answer questions by checking the ingredient sheet rather than guessing. She also asked them to keep the serving spoons separate: one for the stew, one for the rice, and one for the carrots. A volunteer noticed that the handle on the rice spoon had a crack. Mara replaced it from the clean utensil drawer before service began.

The updated message from the shelter arrived at 8:20. It said that 18 additional people would need lunch, including several children, and asked whether the kitchen could send the meals by 11:30. Because the extra rice was still dry and the kitchen had enough lentils and broth, Mara approved cooking another pot. If the shelter had asked for more meals than the pantry could support, the team would have called the community center before changing the menu; in this case, there were enough ingredients, and the community center was not contacted. Two volunteers started the extra rice while Priya increased the stew batch. Mara wrote the new total on the whiteboard and told the packing team not to seal the shelter containers until the food had been counted.

At 9:15, a delivery driver arrived with bread that had been ordered for the following week. The invoice showed the later date, so Mara thanked him but did not accept the delivery into the day’s inventory. She called the bakery, and the manager confirmed that the order had been brought a week early by mistake. The driver took the crates back, leaving the kitchen with its original bread supply. That meant the team did not need to change the meal plan or borrow bread from another organization. Ben checked the remaining bags and found two with torn seams; those were kept for the volunteers’ staff meal, while intact bags were set aside for guests.

Service started at 11:45, fifteen minutes later than the shelter’s requested arrival time. The shelter driver had called to say that traffic was moving slowly near the bridge, so the packed containers stayed in the warming cabinet until the van arrived. The volunteers served guests at the kitchen’s front tables while Mara and Leon counted portions for the delivery. They packed 158 complete lunches, then counted the labels again before loading the van. “We have the right number, and the ingredient sheets are on top,” Leon said. Mara checked that the containers were closed and that the hot-food thermometer still showed a safe temperature. The driver signed the handoff sheet at 12:05 and carried the food to the shelter.

After the lunch rush, the team washed cookware, sanitized the counters, and recorded the remaining food. The lentil stew had run out, while some rice and roasted carrots remained. Mara cooled the leftovers according to the kitchen’s storage procedure, labeled the containers with the date and time, and placed them in the refrigerator. The cracked spoon was marked for disposal, and the delivery discrepancy was noted on the inventory form so the next shift would know why the bread count differed from the invoice. Before leaving, the volunteers checked the floor, emptied the compost bin, and returned the clean serving utensils to their drawer. Mara thanked each person by name and left the whiteboard updated for Sunday’s team: 158 lunches served, one early bread delivery returned, and the remaining rice and carrots stored for later use.

The updated message from the shelter arrived at 8:20. It said that 18 additional people would need lunch, including several children, and asked whether the kitchen could send the meals by 11:30. Because the extra rice was still dry and the kitchen had enough lentils and broth, Mara approved cooking another pot. If the shelter had asked for more meals than the pantry could support, the team would have called the community center before changing the menu; in this case, there were enough ingredients, and the community center was not contacted. Mara wrote the new total on the whiteboard and told the packing team not to seal the shelter containers until the food had been counted.

The invoice showed the later date, so Mara thanked him but did not accept the delivery into the day’s inventory. She called the bakery, and the manager confirmed that the order had been brought a week early by mistake. The driver took the crates back, leaving the kitchen with its original bread supply. That meant the team did not need to change the meal plan or borrow bread from another organization. The shelter driver had called to say that traffic was moving slowly near the bridge, so the packed containers stayed in the warming cabinet until the van arrived. The volunteers served guests at the kitchen’s front tables while Mara and Leon counted portions for the delivery. They packed 158 complete lunches, then counted the labels again before loading the van. “We have the right number, and the ingredient sheets are on top,” Leon said. Mara checked that the containers were closed and that the hot-food thermometer still showed a safe temperature. The driver signed the handoff sheet at 12:05 and carried the food to the shelter.

Mara cooled the leftovers according to the kitchen’s storage procedure, labeled the containers with the date and time, and placed them in the refrigerator. The cracked spoon was marked for disposal, and the delivery discrepancy was noted on the inventory form so the next shift would know why the bread count differed from the invoice. Before leaving, the volunteers checked the floor, emptied the compost bin, and returned the clean serving utensils to their drawer. Mara thanked each person by name and left the whiteboard updated for Sunday’s team: 158 lunches served, one early bread delivery returned, and the remaining rice and carrots stored for later use.

MODE: /polish
LANGUAGE: en
PROFILE: Plain and direct.
INPUT:
The north block of Cedar Lane Orchard uses a low-pressure drip system fed from a lined storage pond. On Monday morning, Mara Chen found a wet strip beside row 18 and a drop in pressure at the far end of the lateral. The pump gauge still showed its usual range, so she checked the filter and the main valve before opening the repair area. The filter screen held a small amount of leaf grit but was not blocked. The valve handle moved freely, and there was no visible leak around its fittings. She recorded the pressure readings and marked the wet ground with two orange flags so the crew could return to the same location after the soil dried.

The affected lateral runs about 110 meters along the lower side of the block. It serves 24 young pear trees and shares a supply manifold with two shorter laterals. The pipe lies under a narrow strip of mulch, with a shallow drainage swale about four meters downhill. The ground was soft from irrigation the previous evening, but there had been no rain for six days. Mara shut the row valve and waited for the line to drain before lifting the mulch. Water continued to seep from one point near a connector, although the rest of the exposed pipe remained dry. That detail suggested a local leak rather than a problem at the manifold.

1. The crew isolated the section between the row valve and the final emitter. Luis Ortega used a hand spade to remove mulch and soil in thin layers, taking care not to pull on the nearby emitter tubing. At a depth of about 12 centimeters, he found a split in the 16-millimeter lateral, roughly 30 centimeters from a barbed coupling. The split was on the underside of the pipe and measured about 18 millimeters. The coupling did not appear cracked, and its barb remained seated. Luis said, “The fitting looks sound; the pipe has opened beside it.” Mara photographed the pipe before cutting it, with a ruler and the row marker visible in the frame.

2. The damaged part was cut out with clean shears. The crew checked the cut ends for flattening and dirt, then trimmed a few millimeters from one end to get a round, clean opening. They used a straight 16-millimeter repair sleeve from the orchard’s parts cabinet and pushed each pipe end fully over the sleeve barbs. The sleeve fit tightly without a clamp. Mara marked the insertion depth with a pencil before joining the pieces, which let her confirm that neither end had shifted while the crew handled the pipe. The repaired length remained aligned with the existing lateral and did not rest against the coupling or a tree stake.

3. Before covering the repair, Mara reopened the row valve slowly. She watched the connection for several minutes while Luis checked the emitter at the end of the line and compared its flow with an emitter on the neighboring row. No water appeared at the cut, and the far-end pressure reading returned close to the measurement from the previous week. The emitter flow looked similar by eye, but the crew did not have a flow meter with them. Mara noted that limitation in the work log rather than recording a measured flow rate. They left the repair exposed during the rest of the test so any new seepage would be easy to see.

4. The soil around the line was still damp, so the crew placed the excavated soil on a tarp instead of piling it against the pipe. They removed two small stones from the trench and checked that the drainage path remained open. The mulch went back only after the repair area stayed dry through a second short test. Luis spread it evenly without pressing it onto the lateral. The orange flags remained in place, and Mara added a small map mark showing the repair’s distance from the row marker. The crew took the tarp and cut pipe back to the equipment shed for disposal and inventory.

The work log includes the date, block, row, pipe size, approximate split length, parts used, and the two pressure readings. Mara attached the before-and-after photographs and noted that the leak was found on the underside of the lateral near the barbed coupling. She also recorded that the screen had leaf grit but was not blocked, since that observation may help if pressure falls again elsewhere in the block. The filter was returned to its housing after inspection, and the main valve remained in its normal operating position. The row valve was left open for scheduled irrigation.

The repair sits in a section where equipment access is limited by the swale and by a line of established pear trees. The tractor cannot pass between the rows when the ground is soft, so the crew brought the spade, shears, sleeve, tarp, and pressure gauge by hand. A shallow rut beside the lower access path had collected water earlier in the season, but it was dry during this visit. Mara asked the crew not to widen the excavation unless the sleeve moved or the leak returned. That kept the disturbed area small and left the nearby feeder roots covered.

During the test, Luis heard a brief hiss from the manifold, then saw that it came from water leaving an air-release point as the line refilled. The sound stopped after the pressure settled. He checked the manifold’s unions and the two neighboring row valves; neither had visible moisture. Mara entered the hiss in her notes because it occurred during the refill, but she did not list it as a leak. If pressure drops again while the filter remains clear, the crew will compare the far-end reading on row 18 with the neighboring rows before opening the repaired section. That condition matters because the shared manifold can affect more than one lateral.

The final inspection covered the pipe alignment, sleeve position, mulch depth, nearby emitters, and the drainage swale. The lateral was not under tension, and the repaired segment had enough room to move slightly with changes in temperature. The two flags and map mark identify the location for a later check without relying on the photographs alone. Mara left the work log in the irrigation shed with the gauge readings and parts count, while the images remained attached to the orchard’s maintenance record. No further excavation was made during this visit, and the surrounding soil was left level with the original grade.

i'm setting up HarborClip on the studio desktop for the weekly archive uploads and want the profile ready for review before i save it. use the profile filename harborclip-weekly.json, and keep incoming files in D:\Studio\Archive\Incoming on the internal drive, not a network share. the operator will start each batch manually, so leave automatic startup off. first, leave original filenames unchanged. second, allow resumable transfers by setting this key to true
transfer.allow_resume
third, set the connection timeout to 30 seconds. allow four retries after the first attempt, with a 10 second wait between retries. don't enable automatic deletion after upload, because i need the local copies for the monthly check. keep the uploader window open after each batch, and show a notice when a transfer fails, not for every successful file. there are usually 12 files in a batch, but that's the current workload, not a limit for the setting. the profile should still accept larger batches when needed. keep the transfer log for 14 days. could you check these values and tell me if any field is missing? please don't save the profile yet. i want to review the configuration first.

payload.instruction:
MODE: /polish
LANGUAGE: en
PROFILE: Clear and professional.
INPUT:
our film society, Lantern Film Society, has started putting together a four-week series called “Rooms We Leave,” and the planning is happening in North Hall, where the club usually meets. There are eleven volunteers involved this term, though not all of them can be at every meeting. The series is for September 12, 19, 26, and October 3, with one screening each evening. We have reserved the North Hall auditorium, which has 84 seats, but the reservation is not a statement that we expect to fill it. The room is also used by the debate team, so our equipment and boxes need to be cleared out after each event.

The program is about interiors and the ways people use them, rather than being a strict historical survey. The first night is planned around two short films from the regional archive, and the next three evenings each have one feature-length film under consideration. We have not yet received the archive’s written confirmation for the second feature. It is in the same broad theme, but it has a quieter pace than the rest, which may make the transition between films a little uneven if we keep the short pair on night one. I think that is manageable, although I would not describe it as a completely settled running order.

Maya Chen is coordinating the archive messages, and she said, “They told me the rights form is in the review queue, not that it has been approved.” That wording matters because volunteers have already asked whether they can put the title on the printed card. We are holding the card design until the society has permission in writing. If written rights confirmation for the second feature has not arrived by August 18, we will replace it with the already licensed short program that Ravi has proposed. This is a contingency, not a decision that the feature has been rejected, and the program note should not describe it as one.

The other three titles are still being compared for fit and cost. The first feature is available through the campus library, but its delivery link expires on October 6, so someone will need to test it before the final screening date and not assume that a link which works in September will keep working. The third title is offered by a small distributor at a student rate, with a separate caption file. We have asked whether the captions are included in that rate, and the reply has not arrived. The fourth evening might use a locally made documentary if the group can confirm that the filmmaker is comfortable with a public campus screening; at present, we only have an informal conversation about that possibility.

There are several practical items beyond choosing the films. Joel will ask facilities to unlock the auditorium at 5:30 p.m. each evening, while the first screening is listed to begin at 6:15. The volunteers need time to check the projector, set out the captioning receiver, and place the program cards near the entrance. The projector sometimes makes skin tones look slightly warm, according to Maya, but she has not tested it with these files yet. We should do a test with a sample file before the first event rather than treating her observation as a confirmed problem with the selected films.

1. Publicity and printed material: Nia is drafting a one-page schedule for the campus noticeboards and a shorter announcement for the society mailing list. The noticeboard version needs the dates, room, start time, and the series title; it should not promise that a particular title will appear until the rights and screening permissions are settled. We usually get more questions about captions than about the film descriptions, so the announcement can mention that caption access is being checked without saying that every file is confirmed. The mailing list will go out after the printed card is approved.

2. Access and seating: The auditorium has a step-free entrance from the east corridor, and four seats can be removed from the front row if wheelchair spaces are needed. The society has not received any seating requests so far. Priya will check the receiver batteries and place a brief instruction card beside the sign-in sheet. She says people occasionally miss the receiver table when it is set too close to the doorway, so it may be better to put it beside the welcome desk. That is a suggestion for the room layout, not a confirmed accommodation request from a guest.

3. Volunteer roles: For each screening, two volunteers will stay near the door, one will manage the projector, and one will keep track of attendance. The remaining people can rotate between greeting guests and restocking the water jug. We do not charge admission, but the society plans to put out a voluntary contribution jar for future license costs. The jar is not connected to entry, and the announcement should make that clear if it mentions contributions. The club has not set a fundraising target for this series.

4. Follow-up and review: After October 3, the committee intends to collect short comments from attendees and review which practical arrangements worked. Ravi suggested a paper slip as well as a QR code because some visitors do not want to use a phone during an event. We have not chosen the questions yet, and no one is being asked to submit a name. The review is meant to help with the next program, not to rank the films or claim that one screening was more successful than another. If the archive confirmation misses the August 18 date, the schedule and the review sheet will both need the replacement program name before they are printed.

The society is keeping the series modest because volunteers also have coursework and other club events during September. We can probably staff the current plan, but the availability sheet has two unanswered entries for October 3, so the committee should not treat that evening’s assignments as complete. The film descriptions can stay brief, with one sentence about each film’s use of space and a note about its source. The final room checklist should include the auditorium key, the projector test, the receiver, the sign-in sheet, and removal of the society’s materials afterward. Facilities has asked that no boxes be left in the corridor overnight, and the debate team needs the auditorium returned in its usual layout. Those details are part of the plan even while the feature choices and the fourth-night permission remain unresolved.

the inventory has six notes first the tin box holds school portraits from the west family branch and its lid has a dent near the hinge second the album with the cloth cover has loose corners but every page is still attached third the two photographs in the glass frame should stay in the frame until uncle ray can bring the soft opening tool fourth the envelope from the lake picnic is stored behind the ledger and not inside it fifth the scan of the orchard group needs a second look because the lower edge is darker than the print sixth the catalogue does not include postcards so the card from mill bay belongs in the separate correspondence folder

The table is still needed for dinner, so I have been moving the folders into the blue crate each afternoon and putting the crate back beside the bookcase before anyone comes over. Nobody has changed the order of the original prints, and the handwritten labels are still facing up.

Grandma Rose began the catalogue in a green ledger in 1988, and Dad added dates in pencil whenever he knew them. The ledger lists the photographer or the person who donated a print, but it does not say that every date is certain. The picture of the three children by the apple shed is marked “about 1951,” and Uncle Peter thinks it may have been taken a year later because the shed roof was repaired in the summer of 1952. We should leave the wording as it is until someone finds a dated copy. The scan folder has a separate note for that question and does not replace the ledger.

This is Mara Ellis, recording the handoff notes for the North Room rehearsal archive on Monday the twelfth of May. The main thing I am doing today is forwarding the reference files and the paper log scans to the Harbor Sound Library. We have forty-two labeled audio files and eleven folders of related documents. The oldest audio file is on a compact disc, and the newest one is a WAV file from February this year. We found thirty-eight cassettes, two mini discs, and four memory cards in the blue case. The cassette labels use pencil, and some are difficult to read, but every label is legible in the close photographs. The shelf list also records three rehearsal dates that were changed by the hall manager, so those dates are not evidence that a session took place. The paper log has a note from Jo Wren saying the youth theatre left the room at six on the seventeenth and the brass group came in after seven. Jo wrote that the door was still unlocked when she returned for her scarf, and that detail is why the key register is included with the other scans.

Numbered notes for the transfer. Item one: the folder called North Room Brass includes rehearsal plans for the winter concert. Item two: the folder called Youth Theatre includes a running order and a cast list with phone numbers covered before the copy was made. Item three: the small envelope marked Room Tone has two audio files and a handwritten note that says, “Do not reduce the low hum because it is part of the room recording.” The note is signed by Lena Cho, who recorded the files. Item four: the blue case inventory has one blank line where the last memory card should have a description. The card itself is marked “April lobby,” and I have kept that wording rather than guessing what lobby means. The archive reference for this transfer is HS North 24 051, and the scan folder uses the same reference.

Ravi at the Harbor Sound Library asked for the files in their original folder order and for the log pages to remain separate from the rehearsal plans. I am forwarding a copy of the shelf list as well as the scans because the list gives the date and location for each item. The scanner glass picked up a faint line on the next page, and the line appears in the image too. The paper is cream rather than white, so the background looks darker than the pages in the newer folder. Nothing has been removed from the scan set, and the two pages with personal phone numbers are the versions with those numbers covered.

The checksum sheet lists the source filename, the copy filename, the file size, and the date of the copy. The original names are retained in a column because two files have the same rehearsal date but different start times. The document folder contains the photographed cassette labels, the booking sheets, the key register, the shelf list, and the log pages. The rehearsal plans are filed after the related booking sheet rather than by the date they were scanned. LANGUAGE: en
PROFILE: Friendly and conversational.
INPUT:
The family photo catalogue brings together images from the Mercer family’s boxes, albums, envelopes, and a small group of digital files. It covers gatherings from 1948 through 2019, with the largest clusters documenting summer visits to Lake Erie, birthdays at the Cedar Street house, and Sunday dinners hosted by Ruth and Daniel Mercer. The catalogue is meant to help relatives find and understand photographs, not to rank them or decide which memories matter most. Each entry identifies what can be seen, gives the best available date and location, and notes who supplied the image or information.

The oldest photographs are mostly black-and-white prints mounted in three albums that belonged to Ruth’s parents. Their handwritten captions include names, dates, and occasional place names, although the writing is not always easy to read. The catalogue retains a transcription when the wording is clear and marks uncertain readings with a question mark. A note beside a photograph dated 1952 reads, “Mildred and the cousins after the rain.” No one has established which cousins are shown, so the entry identifies Mildred and describes the remaining people without assigning names. The photograph’s paper frame gives the date a little more support than the caption alone.

Later collections include loose colour prints, photo-booth strips, slides, and several folders of phone pictures. Many loose prints were originally grouped by event, but a few envelopes have no writing and may have been mixed during a house move. The catalogue records the envelope and box in which each item was found when that detail is available. Digital copies retain their original filenames in a separate field, while catalogue entries use a consistent family-friendly title. This makes the images easier to browse without hiding the names that came with them.

The catalogue uses a small number of practical conventions. Dates can be exact, approximate, or unknown; a month or season is included when it is more reliable than a guessed day. Locations are recorded at the level supported by the evidence, such as “Cedar Street kitchen” or “near Toledo,” rather than being made more precise for neatness. A person’s name is included only when someone can identify the person or a caption supplies the name. If relatives disagree, both accounts are recorded with their sources instead of choosing one by default. These conventions keep the entries readable while leaving room for later corrections.

1. Each entry has a catalogue number, a short title, a date or date range, a location, and a description of the visible scene. The source field identifies an album, envelope, donor, or digital folder whenever that information is known. A separate people field lists confirmed names and notes uncertain identifications. The catalogue number stays attached to the image even if its title or date changes, so printed references and family messages remain useful after an edit.

2. Scans are stored as archival files and as smaller copies for the family’s shared browsing folder. The archival copy keeps the full image area, including borders, handwritten notes, and marks on the back when those details are relevant. A crop may be made for a display page, but it does not replace the uncropped scan. The entry links both versions and notes when a crop has been used. Slide scans are also linked to a record of the original slide mount, since a handwritten label on the mount may provide information that is not visible in the projected image.

3. The catalogue keeps a record of its working notes in the file named below. That record lists questions that remain open, explains changes to names or dates, and gives the date of each edit. A family member can therefore see why an entry changed without having to compare successive copies by eye.

north-gate-notes.md

4. Access is arranged by collection rather than by a blanket rule for every image. Relatives can browse the family folder, while scans that show private correspondence or sensitive personal details are kept in a restricted folder. If a photograph’s location is uncertain and the image could reveal a private home address, the entry stays out of the shared browsing folder until that location has been checked. The catalogue can still retain a restricted record of the image and the reason for the temporary limit. INPUT:

our working plan for the North Quad Film Society's October program is to hold three Thursday screenings, on October 8, October 15, and October 22, 2026. This is still a proposed schedule, not a confirmed booking. The first film is City in Rain, with a running time of 84 minutes; the second is a group of shorts called Paper Moons, with a combined running time of 47 minutes; and the third is Last Stop, which runs for 91 minutes. We are asking the campus events office to reserve room B214 for each date. The room has 92 seats, and the film society would like to keep 12 of them available for students who arrive without registering. Doors are planned to open at 6:15 p.m., with each screening starting at 6:45 p.m. The start time should stay the same on all three dates, so students do not have to interpret a different schedule every week.

The draft schedule leaves room for a brief welcome before each screening, but it does not include a discussion afterward. For City in Rain, the film's distributor has quoted a runtime of 84 minutes, while the copy in the society's archive lists 83 minutes. The program coordinator is asking the distributor to verify which runtime should go on the public listing; until they reply, the 84-minute figure is the one in this draft. Paper Moons is made up of four shorts, and the 47-minute figure is the combined runtime supplied by the filmmaker. Last Stop has a 91-minute runtime on its licensing sheet. These times do not include introductions, and the society has not promised that every screening will finish at a particular time. The draft assumes that the welcome will take no more than five minutes, but it remains a planning estimate.

Room B214 is on the second floor of North Quad Hall. The building entrance on Cedar Walk has a ramp, and the events office directory lists an elevator near the east stairwell. We are asking the office to confirm that the elevator will be operating on all three evenings and that the room's aisle layout can accommodate a wheelchair user without blocking an exit. The society's access lead, Mina Patel, has also asked whether the room can be unlocked 30 minutes before doors open, so volunteers have time to check the projector and place the printed program sheets. If the room cannot be opened by 5:45 p.m., the access lead wants the society to move the equipment check to the student lounge rather than shorten the planned check. That is a request for the events office to consider, not a confirmed alternative booking.

The volunteer plan is organized around four roles, with the same assignments expected to apply on each date unless a volunteer reports a conflict.
1. The program coordinator will introduce the film and give the welcome. The coordinator is also responsible for checking that the announced running time matches the public listing once the distributor confirms the figure for City in Rain.
2. Two door volunteers will check student IDs and count attendance. They should record the number of people entering, not the number of seats left, and they should keep the 12 walk-in seats visible on the seating chart until the screening begins. The society has not decided whether any unused reserved seats will be released early.
3. One projection volunteer will test the playback file and sound level before doors open. For Paper Moons, that person should check all four shorts in their listed order and confirm that the combined file does not begin with the filmmaker's slate. The filmmaker has said, "the slate is for review, not for the audience," and the society is asking whether a version without the slate can be provided.
4. One access volunteer will keep the ramp-side aisle clear and bring the large-print program sheets to the entrance. The society has printed 18 large-print copies, based on requests received so far, but that number is not a cap on requests at the door.

The room request should be tracked under the filename below, because the campus events office asked the society to use one filename for the attendance estimate and equipment notes. The file is a working document, not a confirmed room reservation. The current estimate is 74 attendees on October 8, 68 on October 15, and 80 on October 22. Each number is an estimate for that date, not a count of registrations. The equipment notes ask for one HDMI cable, two handheld microphones, and a standing lamp at the entrance. The projection volunteer has already checked that the society owns one HDMI adapter, but has not checked whether it works with the room's projector.

delivery-summary.tsv

For publicity, the society is preparing one digital poster and 60 printed copies for the student center and the library noticeboard. The poster draft includes all three dates, the 6:45 p.m. start time, and a note that admission is free for currently enrolled students. The society is asking the communications desk to review the poster's use of the college wordmark before printing. The wordmark is not yet cleared for this use. The student center allows posters on the north display panel, while the library noticeboard requires approval from its desk staff; volunteers should not assume that permission for one location covers the other. The society would like to post the digital version on September 21, if the wordmark review is complete by then. If the review is still pending on September 21, the coordinator wants to hold the digital post and use a text-only listing in the weekly bulletin instead. The printed copies are to wait until the wordmark question is resolved, even if that means they are not available for the first week of publicity.

The draft budget lists $180 for the three screening licenses, $36 for printing, and $24 for refreshments. The $180 license figure is the total quoted amount, not a per-film amount; it covers the three listed program dates, subject to the distributor's final confirmation of the City in Rain runtime. The printing figure covers 60 standard copies and 18 large-print copies, and the society has asked the campus print desk whether both sizes can be charged to the same order. The refreshments amount is a ceiling for bottled water and packaged snacks, not an instruction to spend the full amount. The treasurer has asked the student activities office whether the society may use its remaining $90 from the fall events allocation toward these costs. That balance is recorded in the society's spreadsheet, but the office has not confirmed that it is available for this program. Until there is a reply, the $90 should remain a possible contribution rather than being subtracted from the total budget request.

The society is also checking whether a short introduction by filmmaker Jo Alvarez is possible for the October 15 program. Alvarez's assistant said, "Jo may be in town that week, but we cannot confirm a visit yet." The coordinator is asking the assistant to confirm availability by September 28. No travel or appearance payment is included in the current budget, and the society has not asked Alvarez to attend remotely. If the assistant confirms a visit, the coordinator wants to ask the events office whether the room can be entered 15 minutes earlier that evening; if there is no confirmation by September 28, the screening should continue with the standard welcome by the program coordinator. The draft should therefore leave Alvarez's name out of the public poster for now, while keeping the possible introduction in the internal schedule notes.

The remaining planning questions are the distributor's confirmed runtime for City in Rain, the operation of the elevator, the room's early-unlock time, the wordmark review, and whether the $90 allocation can be used. Mina Patel is following up with the events office about access and room opening, while the program coordinator is handling the distributor and publicity questions. The treasurer will contact the student activities office about the allocation. The society wants those separate replies recorded against the relevant dates and costs, rather than treating any pending item as settled. The October 8 attendance estimate of 74 should remain in the working file until registration opens, and the door volunteers will use the actual entry count on the evening itself. The room booking, equipment request, and public listing are still being prepared from this draft, with the October dates and shared 6:45 p.m. start time as the basis for the requests.
